										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Ukraine&#8217;s parliament is considering <a href="https://itd.rada.gov.ua/billinfo/Bills/Card/70736" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Draft Law No. 16069 of 14 September 2026</a>, which proposes amendments to the Tax Code of Ukraine to reduce VAT rates on food products, medicines, children&#8217;s items and other socially significant goods, and to lower costs for consumers. Subject to approval, the law will apply from 1 January 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Permanent 5% rate</strong></p>
<p>The draft law adds subparagraph &#8220;ґ&#8221; to paragraph 193.1 of Article 193 of the Tax Code, introducing a 5% VAT rate on the following categories.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Medicines and medical products</strong>:
<ul>
<li>registered medicines and medical devices meeting official technical regulations;</li>
<li>medicines and equipment used in clinical trials authorised by the Ministry of Health;</li>
<li>unregistered medicines imported under expanded patient access programmes, including their subsequent free distribution to healthcare providers and participating patients; and</li>
<li>preserved or compounded medicines prepared directly in pharmacies according to doctors&#8217; prescriptions or orders from healthcare facilities.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Specialised and children&#8217;s items</strong>:
<ul>
<li>foods intended for special medical purposes and sanitary hygiene products, according to a list established by the Cabinet of Ministers; and</li>
<li>baby food, child car seats, strollers, slings, ergonomic backpacks, children&#8217;s tableware, basic clothing, footwear and educational stationery.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Socially significant food products</strong>:
<ul>
<li>fresh or chilled meat and edible offal (excluding certain industrial categories);</li>
<li>fresh, chilled or frozen fish (excluding industrial supply);</li>
<li>milk, dairy products, eggs and natural honey (excluding items with added chocolate, alcohol or confectionery);</li>
<li>vegetables, fruits and nuts (excluding seed or feed material and candied or glazed products); and</li>
<li>coffee, tea, spices, retail-packaged cereals, flour, groats, sunflower oil, olive oil, sugar, cocoa powder, pasta, bakery products, yeast, seasonings, pre-packaged water and salt.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>The current VAT rate on medical products and pharmaceuticals is 7%. The draft law would permanently reduce it to 5% and expand the scope to cover pharmacy-made medicines, specialised dietary foods for medical purposes, sanitary hygiene products and certain children&#8217;s goods.</p>
<p>The permanent 5% rate would also apply to core grocery items from the consumer basket, including meat, fish, dairy, vegetables, fruits, flour, cereals, cooking oil, bread and pasta.</p>
<p><strong>Temporary 7% rate</strong></p>
<p>A new clause, Point 101 of Subsection 2 of Section XX, establishes a temporary reduced 7% VAT rate on goods that support household needs during power outages and blackouts. It will apply until Ukraine achieves full membership in the European Union (EU). The goods covered are:</p>
<ul>
<li>Household emergency items: candles, matches, disinfectants, portable gas stoves and burners, gas cartridges, primary batteries, flashlights and lanterns.</li>
<li>Power equipment: backup power equipment, including electric generator sets, static converters and inverters (excluding inverter welding machines), and lithium-ion storage batteries.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Tax Code and implementation</strong></p>
<p>The draft law updates Article 194.1 of the Tax Code to integrate the 5%, 7% and 14% rates alongside the standard 20% rate into the base tax system.</p>
<p>The Law is scheduled to come into force on 1 January 2027.</p>
<p>The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine will have three months from publication of the law to adopt the necessary subordinate regulations and align existing ministerial acts.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>France&#8217;s National Assembly published the<a href="https://www.assemblee-nationale.fr/dyn/17/textes/l17b3210_projet-loi" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> draft Finance Bill for 2027</a> on 1 October 2026, outlining the government&#8217;s plan to lower the public deficit from a revised 5.4% of GDP in 2026 to 5.0% in 2027, subject to parliamentary approval.</p>
<p>The measures would generally apply from 1 January 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Corporate taxation</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>The temporary surtax on corporate income tax would run for a further year for companies with turnover of at least EUR 1.5 billion. The rates would be lower, at 15.7% for turnover up to EUR 3 billion and 31.4% above that.</li>
<li>The exceptional tax on large maritime shipping companies under the tonnage tax regime would return at a reduced rate of 8%. It would apply to companies with annual global turnover of EUR 1 billion or more, for fiscal years closing on or after 31 December 2026.</li>
<li>A temporary &#8220;Industry 4.0&#8221; super-depreciation scheme would cover advanced manufacturing, automation and digital assets ordered between 2027 and 2029.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Pillar Two</strong></p>
<p>General-interest social housing activities would be excluded from qualified results under the GloBE rules. Their income is generally exempt and could otherwise push the ETR below 15% for QDMTT purposes.</p>
<p><strong>VAT</strong></p>
<p>Streaming platforms and composite telecom/TV bundles would face the standard VAT rate of 20%.</p>
<p><strong>Tax administration</strong></p>
<p>Authorities would receive permanent powers for automated data collection and web scraping of online platform content. The aim is to detect unreported income and false tax residences.</p>
<p><strong>Personal taxation</strong></p>
<p>The bill indexes the personal income tax brackets for inflation. The general rates are 0% up to EUR 11,844, 11% up to EUR 30,200, 30% up to EUR 86,353, 41% up to EUR 185,737 and 45% above that. The government says indexation shields about 20 million households from an aggregate increase of nearly EUR 4 billion.</p>
<p>The bill also sets a EUR 3,000 sub-cap on the 10% pension deduction.</p>
<p><strong>Deficit and growth outlook</strong></p>
<p>The government has cut its 2026 growth estimate to 0.5% from 1.0%, citing Middle East tensions and summer droughts. The consolidation effort relies on EUR 43 billion in recovery measures across the Finance Bill and the Social Security Finance Bill.</p>
<p><strong>Public spending</strong></p>
<p>State spending under the expenditure norm would remain frozen at EUR 511 billion, with defence receiving an extra EUR 6.4 billion. The bill also proposes a temporary contribution on local government tax revenues, expected to raise EUR 2.5 billion.</p>
<p>The proposals will now go through parliamentary scrutiny before any of the measures can take effect from 1 January 2027.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/france-considers-2027-finance-bill-with-cit-surcharge-green-tax-measures/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, the French government presented the Finance Bill for 2027 to the National Assembly on 1 October 2026 for parliamentary consideration.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[Finland’s government has submitted a legislative proposal (HE 211/2026) to Parliament to amend the existing rules on mergers on 1 October 2026. The proposal aims to make corporate restructuring rules more flexible, streamline tax procedures, and reduce the administrative burden on taxpayers and the Tax Administration. Key reforms include enabling tax-neutral sister company mergers, introducing...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Finland’s government has <a href="https://www.eduskunta.fi/fi/asiat-ja-aanestykset/valtiopaivaasiat/asiakirjat/edktunnus/EDK-2026-AK-50518" target="_blank" rel="noopener">submitted</a> a legislative proposal (HE 211/2026) to Parliament to amend the existing rules on mergers on 1 October 2026. The proposal aims to make corporate restructuring rules more flexible, streamline tax procedures, and reduce the administrative burden on taxpayers and the Tax Administration.</p>
<p>Key reforms include enabling tax-neutral sister company mergers, introducing demergers executed through incorporation, and adjusting the maximum limit for cash consideration up to 50%. Additionally, the text outlines updates regarding negative net contributions in business transfers, rules for loss deductions within corporate groups, and the calculation of mathematical values for shares during mergers, demergers, and share issuances.</p>
<p>The amendments are set to take effect on 1 January 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Tax-neutral mergers without consideration and indirect ownership </strong></p>
<p>The proposed amendment would expand tax-neutral merger treatment without consideration to certain indirect sister-company mergers. It would permit such mergers where shareholders indirectly own the receiving company through a 100%-owned intermediate company, but the relief would be limited to one intermediate ownership tier to ensure predictability and prevent changes in shareholder ownership proportions.</p>
<p><strong>Proposed changes to demerger structures and share valuation</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Demerger via incorporation: </strong>A new demerger form would allow a company to transfer one or more business units to a newly incorporated entity in exchange for shares issued to the demerging company itself. Unlike a business transfer, this operates as universal succession, automatically transferring contracts, liabilities, and tax losses.</li>
<li><strong>Share consideration for real estate and housing companies: </strong>The amendment would relax the proportional distribution rule for housing and mutual real estate companies. Shareholders could receive shares only in the receiving entity that takes over the property or apartment rights linked to their original shares.</li>
<li><strong>Acquisition cost for listed companies:</strong> Where all companies involved in a demerger are publicly listed, the original shares’ acquisition cost would be allocated based on their relative fair market values, using initial stock exchange trading prices rather than net asset values.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Increase in maximum cash consideration</strong></p>
<p>The proposed amendment would increase the maximum cash consideration allowed in tax-neutral mergers and demergers from 10% to 50%. Where consideration shares have no nominal value, the 50% limit would be calculated based on total paid-in equity, including SVOP funds, rather than only share capital.</p>
<p><strong>Tax-neutral business transfers with negative net assets</strong></p>
<p>The reform would allow tax-neutral business transfers even where the transferred assets have a negative net tax value, overturning earlier restrictions such as KHO 2001:3. The negative value would result in a negative acquisition cost for the consideration shares. On a later sale, this amount would increase the taxable gain. Even where the share sale is otherwise tax-exempt under EVL 6 b §, the amount corresponding to the negative acquisition cost would remain taxable to prevent untaxed value accrual.</p>
<p><strong>Clarification of EEA scope</strong></p>
<p>The reform would codify established Supreme Administrative Court case law and clarify that tax-neutral restructuring rules under EVL 52 § 2 and EVL 52 e § apply to corporate entities throughout the European Economic Area (EEA), in line with EU/EEA principles on freedom of establishment and free movement of capital.</p>
<p><strong>Group loss deductibility in mergers and demergers</strong></p>
<p>The reform would allow a receiving company to deduct confirmed tax losses of a merged or demerged company where both entities have belonged to the same corporate group since the beginning of the loss-making year, removing the need for a separate exception permit in certain group restructurings.</p>
<p><strong>Mathematical value for non-listed dividend taxation</strong></p>
<p>The rules would clarify that the mathematical value used to determine the 8% dividend threshold for non-listed companies is the latest value calculated at the end of the tax year, including where restructurings occur during the year.</p>
<p><strong>Recalculation in restructurings and share issues</strong></p>
<p>Mathematical values would be recalculated for the tax year of a merger or demerger regardless of financial year-end or dividend timing. For share issues, new shares would receive a mathematical value only after registration in the Trade Register, and invested funds would be included in net assets from the tax year of registration.</p>
<p><strong>Negative net non-cash contributions in valuation</strong></p>
<p>Shares received in a business transfer involving a negative net contribution would have a mathematical value and comparison value of EUR 0. Negative contribution amounts would reduce the parent company’s net assets, but individual share values could not fall below zero.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

Issuing and receiving obligations From 1 January 2027, entities subject to bookkeeping obligations must issue electronic invoices when selling goods and services to other entities...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Norway&#8217;s Tax Directorate adopted the <a href="https://lovdata.no/dokument/SF/forskrift/2026-09-29-1933" target="_blank" rel="noopener">amendments</a> on 29 September 2026, supplementing the changes made to the Bookkeeping Act on 19 June 2026, which introduced mandatory digital bookkeeping and B2B e-invoicing.</p>
<p><strong>Issuing and receiving obligations</strong></p>
<p>From 1 January 2027, entities subject to bookkeeping obligations must issue electronic invoices when selling goods and services to other entities subject to bookkeeping obligations.</p>
<p>Until 1 January 2030, however, this obligation will in practice apply only where the recipient can receive such invoices, typically through registration in ELMA/Peppol. The obligation to receive electronic invoices will be introduced on 1 January 2030.</p>
<p><strong>Approved formats</strong></p>
<p>The approved standards from January 2027 are EHF Invoicing, Peppol BIS Billing, EHF Self-Billing and Peppol BIS Self-Billing, each in version 3.0 or later. During the transition period, other formats such as EDIFACT and E2B may still be used if they meet the Act&#8217;s definition of an electronic invoice. PDF invoices do not qualify and cannot be used where a buyer subject to bookkeeping obligations can receive electronic invoices.</p>
<p><strong>Bookkeeping changes and exemptions</strong></p>
<p>From 1 January 2027, the exemption for bookkeeping-obligated businesses with turnover below NOK 5 million from keeping booked information electronically accessible is repealed.</p>
<p>From 1 January 2028, the buyer&#8217;s organisation number must be stated on the sales document where the buyer is a bookkeeping-obligated business. From 1 January 2030, bookkeeping must be carried out in a digital bookkeeping system, unless the ministry has determined otherwise.</p>
<p>Businesses with turnover not exceeding NOK 50,000 are exempt from digital bookkeeping and from receiving electronic invoices, but must use the electronic format if their invoicing system supports it. Separate exemptions apply to certain financial, insurance and pension activities and to some bankruptcy estates.</p>
<p><strong>Wider context</strong></p>
<p>The staged approach lets existing business capabilities and formats bridge the three years to full digital invoicing and bookkeeping from 2030. It also fits the wider European move towards structured transaction data and digital accounting, including the EU&#8217;s VAT in the Digital Age reforms taking effect from July 2030.</p>

		<title>Slovak Republic issues guidance on advance pricing agreement procedures</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/slovak-republic-issues-guidance-on-advance-pricing-agreement-procedures/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=slovak-republic-issues-guidance-on-advance-pricing-agreement-procedures</link>

				<category><![CDATA[General rules]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Europe]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Slovak Republic]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=89182</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The Slovak Republic’s tax authorities have issued guidance under No. 4/MZ/2026/MU  on 23 September 2026 (the Slovak version was issued on 5 August 2026) that outlines the application process and regulatory framework for Advance Pricing Arrangements (APAs) pursuant to domestic tax legislation. The guidance also details the procedural stages required for taxpayers to obtain advance...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Slovak Republic’s tax authorities have issued <a href="https://www.financnasprava.sk/_img/pfsedit/Dokumenty_PFS/Zverejnovanie_dok/Dane/Metodicke_usmernenia/Medzinarodne_zdanovanie/2026/2026.09.23_004_MZ_MU_ENG.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance under No. 4/MZ/2026/MU</a>  on 23 September 2026 (the Slovak version was<a href="https://www.financnasprava.sk/_img/pfsedit/Dokumenty_PFS/Zverejnovanie_dok/Dane/Metodicke_usmernenia/Medzinarodne_zdanovanie/2026/2026.08.05_004_MZ_2026_MU.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> issued</a> on 5 August 2026) that outlines the application process and regulatory framework for Advance Pricing Arrangements (APAs) pursuant to domestic tax legislation.</p>
<p>The guidance also details the procedural stages required for taxpayers to obtain advance approval for specific transfer pricing methods involving related-party transactions, ensuring alignment with the arm&#8217;s length principle and international standards.</p>
<p>Key statutory features include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Dispute prevention:</strong> Functions as a dispute prevention mechanism to provide certainty that proposed pricing meets the arm&#8217;s length principle.</li>
<li><strong>Eligible pricing methods:</strong> Taxpayers may apply for traditional transaction methods, transactional profit methods, a combination thereof, or any other appropriate method, provided it achieves a reliable arm&#8217;s length result.</li>
</ul>
<p>Other key measures of the guidance are as follows:</p>
<p><strong>Alignment with international standards</strong></p>
<p>The guidance aligns Slovak administrative practices with international transfer pricing standards, including Article 9 of the OECD Model Tax Convention, the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines on Advance Pricing Arrangements, and EU Joint Transfer Pricing Forum recommendations.</p>
<p><strong>Categories of APAs</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers in Slovakia can choose unilateral, bilateral, or multilateral APAs based on the jurisdictions involved. Bilateral and multilateral APAs are handled through the MAP under Article 25 of the OECD Model Tax Convention, with the Slovak Ministry of Finance negotiating with foreign tax authorities. These APAs help prevent economic double taxation and double non-taxation.</p>
<p><strong>Scope of application &amp; aggregation rules</strong></p>
<p>An APA request is initiated solely by the taxpayer. The request must cover a single controlled transaction or a group of transactions assessed on an aggregated basis:</p>
<ul>
<li>Aggregation criteria: Controlled transactions may be grouped into a single request only if they are of a similar nature, executed under comparable conditions, closely linked, or involve comparable functions, assets, and risks. Aggregation must be fully justified within the transfer pricing documentation following Ministry of Finance guidelines.</li>
<li>Separate requests: Transactions failing aggregation criteria require separate APA filings, each attracting an independent filing fee.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>The 7-stage APA process</strong></p>
<p>The Slovak APA procedure consists of seven administrative stages:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Data collection:</strong> The taxpayer gathers the required financial, operational, and internal information.</li>
<li><strong>Pre-filing meeting:</strong> An optional but recommended discussion with the tax authority to address filing requirements and potential issues.</li>
<li><strong>Submission of request:</strong> The taxpayer files the APA request at least 60 days before the relevant tax period, including transaction details, transfer pricing documentation, methodology, and critical assumptions.</li>
<li><strong>Payment monitoring: </strong>The tax authority verifies payment of the required filing fees.</li>
<li><strong>Analysis and evaluation: </strong>The authority assesses the proposed methodology and benchmarking for arm’s-length compliance and may request adjustments.</li>
<li><strong>Decision or notice:</strong> An APA generally applies for up to five tax periods, with possible extensions. Bilateral and multilateral APAs may have longer terms and allow rollback. Decisions are effective from the start of the requested period and cannot be appealed.</li>
<li><strong>Monitoring, changes, or revocation:</strong> The tax authority monitors compliance with critical assumptions. Changes may result in prospective amendment or revocation, while false information can lead to retroactive revocation.</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>Filing fees, reliability reductions, &amp; payment details</strong></p>
<p>Under Section 18(7), APA filing fees are EUR 10,000 for unilateral APAs and EUR 30,000 for bilateral or multilateral APAs. Taxpayers with a “highly reliable” tax reliability rating receive a 50% discount, reducing the fees to EUR 5,000 and EUR 15,000, respectively.</p>
<p><strong>Payment rules</strong></p>
<p>APA fees are payable upon submission and are charged regardless of the outcome. If unpaid, the taxpayer receives a 15-day period to make payment, after which the application is deemed not filed, and any partial payment is refunded. However, fees are non-refundable if the APA request is rejected after formal review.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

The bill was submitted to the Legislative Assembly on 22 September 2026 and proposes a significant structural reform to Costa Rica&#8217;s taxation of foreign-source passive income by shifting from a group-specific rule to a general rule based on fiscal residence....]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Costa Rica published draft Bill No. 25.796 in the <a href="https://www.imprentanacional.go.cr/pub/2026/09/30/ALCA130_30_09_2026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Official Gazette</a> on 30 September 2026. The bill was submitted to the Legislative Assembly on 22 September 2026 and proposes a significant structural reform to Costa Rica&#8217;s taxation of foreign-source passive income by shifting from a group-specific rule to a general rule based on fiscal residence. The initiative modifies the taxation of foreign-source passive income by shifting the focus toward the resident taxpayer&#8217;s economic capacity rather than restricting the levy to multinational corporate entities. To prevent international double taxation, the new regulations allow residents to deduct similar taxes already paid abroad from their net taxable income.</p>
<p><strong>Rationale and context</strong></p>
<p>Bill No. 25,796 would eliminate existing tax asymmetries in the treatment of foreign-source passive income by removing requirements based on multinational group membership, entity qualification, and economic substance. Instead, taxation would be determined primarily by fiscal residence. The reform also aims to address tax erosion concerns arising from the removal of the economic linkage criterion.</p>
<p><strong>Taxpayer scope and covered income</strong></p>
<p>The proposed rules would apply to all Costa Rican tax residents, including individuals, companies, trusts, investment funds, and other entities. They would cover foreign-source passive income from rentals, interest, dividends, royalties, and capital gains on assets or rights located or used outside Costa Rica.</p>
<p>Royalties would expressly include payments for patents, trademarks, copyrights, formulas, and technology transfers, but exclude technical assistance. Covered capital income and gains would be subject to a 15% tax rate.</p>
<p><strong>Double taxation mitigation &amp; capital losses</strong></p>
<p>The proposed rules would calculate taxable foreign passive income on a net basis, allowing foreign taxes paid or withheld to be deducted from gross income to reduce double taxation.</p>
<p>For business and CONASSIF-supervised financial entities, covered foreign passive income would be integrated into gross corporate income and taxed under the general corporate tax regime after the foreign tax deduction.</p>
<p>However, foreign capital losses could not be used to offset domestic tax liabilities.</p>
<p><strong>Targeted scope vs. general territoriality</strong></p>
<p>The proposal is not a shift to a general worldwide income tax system. Active business income remains subject to Costa Rica&#8217;s traditional territoriality principle.</p>
<p><strong>Repeal of thematic bond tax credits</strong></p>
<p>The bill repeals Article 15(d) of Law No. 7092 (introduced by Law No. 10.051), removing the corporate income tax credit previously granted to issuers of thematic (green/sustainable) public offer bonds to restore fiscal neutrality across security issuers.</p>
<p>As drafted, the legislation would enter into force upon approval and publication, with implementing regulations to be issued within six months.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US Trade Representative (USTR) <a href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/october/ustr-seeks-public-comment-2027-joint-review-usmca" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> a formal public consultation for the 2027 USMCA Annual Joint Review on 2 October 2026, seeking written feedback and oral testimony from stakeholders on the trade agreement among the United States, Mexico, and Canada (USMCA).</p>
<p><strong>Submission requirements and deadlines</strong></p>
<p>The USTR established 12 January 2027 at 11:59 p.m. EST as the deadline for all written comments and requests to testify.</p>
<p>Individuals and organisations must file materials through the online portal at <a href="http://comments.ustr.gov" target="_blank" rel="noopener">comments.ustr.gov</a>. Written comments go to docket USTR-2026-0595, while hearing appearance requests go to docket USTR-2026-0596.</p>
<p>The public hearing will take place at a date and location to be announced on the USTR website. Each speaker will receive five minutes for oral testimony. Participants can submit rebuttal comments within seven calendar days after the hearing concludes.</p>
<p><strong>Topics for feedback</strong></p>
<p>The USTR is accepting input on four areas: how the USMCA operates and functions, specific policy recommendations for the joint review, regional competitiveness and investment conditions, and strategies to strengthen economic security against non-market practices from outside countries.</p>
<p>All submissions must be in English. Materials containing confidential business information require clear labelling and a public version. Small businesses with fewer than 500 employees should identify themselves in their submissions.</p>
<p><strong>What happened at the initial review</strong></p>
<p>According to the Federal Register <a href="https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/files/Press/Releases/USMCA%20FRN%2010.2.26.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">notice</a>, the USMCA became effective on 1 July 2020 and carries a 16-year term set to expire on 1 July 2036. The three countries held their first joint review meeting on 1 July 2026. During that meeting, the US<a href="https://regfollower.com/us-walks-away-from-usmca-renewal-eyes-major-trade-overhaul/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> declined </a>to approve an automatic 16-year extension of the pact. This decision triggered a new process that fundamentally changes how the agreement will be governed going forward.</p>
<p><strong>The new annual review schedule</strong></p>
<p>Because the initial extension failed, all three nations must now conduct yearly joint reviews. This continues until either all three countries agree to extend the agreement or it reaches its expiration date in 2036. The public consultation being announced is part of preparation for the 2027 annual review. The trade agreement currently covers USD 1.3 trillion in annual trade among the three countries, making these reviews significant for businesses and workers across North America.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Cyprus Taxation Department, in a <a href="https://www.gov.cy/oikonomia/anakoinosi-tou-tmimatos-forologias-gia-tin-epivoli-midenikou-syntelesti-fpa-se-vasika-eidi/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">release</a> on 2 October 2026, announced a temporary reduction in value-added tax on basic food items and staples, effective from different dates through 31 May 2027.</p>
<p>The decision follows <a href="https://www.gov.cy/media/sites/167/2026/01/%CE%9A.%CE%94.%CE%A0.-354_2026-%CE%A4%CF%81%CE%BF%CF%80%CE%BF%CF%80%CE%BF%CE%AF%CE%B7%CF%83%CE%B7-%CF%84%CE%BF%CF%85-%CE%A0%CE%AD%CE%BC%CF%80%CF%84%CE%BF%CF%85-%CE%BA%CE%B1%CE%B9-%CE%88%CE%BA%CF%84%CE%BF%CF%85-%CE%A0%CE%B1%CF%81%CE%B1%CF%81%CF%84%CE%AE%CE%BC%CE%B1%CF%84%CE%BF%CF%82.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Decree K.D.P. 354/2026</a>, published in the Official Gazette of the Republic (Gazette III Part I, No. 6050, dated 30 September 2026) by order of the Council of Ministers.</p>
<p><strong>Fresh meat and fish: zero VAT from 1 October</strong></p>
<p>Starting 1 October 2026, all fresh, chilled, and frozen meat becomes subject to zero VAT. This applies to beef (CN codes 0201 and 0202), pork (CN code 0203), and lamb and goat meat (CN code 0204). Poultry and rabbit meat also qualify (CN codes 0207 and ex 0208), as do edible offal from these animals (CN code ex 0206).</p>
<p>Fresh and frozen fish products receive the same zero rate, covering standard fish varieties (CN codes 0302, 0303, and 0304) as well as cuttlefish, squid, and octopus (CN code ex 0307).</p>
<p>An important distinction: processed meat and fish remain taxed at 5%. This includes marinated meats, smoked varieties, sausages, canned fish, breaded fish, and similar prepared items.</p>
<p><strong>Bread, milk, coffee, sugar, and baby food: zero VAT from 12 October</strong></p>
<p>A second set of basic items enters the zero VAT zone on 12 October 2026. All fresh or frozen bread qualifies, including white, black, wholemeal, multigrain, and speciality types like baguettes and ciabatta. The exemption excludes pastries, dried bread, and breads with added ingredients such as nuts or raisins.</p>
<p>Milk products eligible for zero VAT encompass cow&#8217;s milk, goat&#8217;s milk, sheep&#8217;s milk, condensed varieties, long-life milk, and plant-based alternatives like almond and soy milk. Instant coffee, roasted beans, ground coffee, and powdered varieties all receive zero VAT, but ready-made coffee drinks remain outside this measure.</p>
<p>Sugar in all forms enters the zero-rate category: granulated, icing, coarse, cubes, and individual sachets. Baby food in powder, dry, or liquid form also qualifies. Snacks such as chocolate, ice cream, and yoghurt remain unaffected by the tax change.</p>
<p>All these provisions end on 31 May 2027.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Nigeria’s Federal Ministry of Finance has introduced new rules for calculating interest on unpaid taxes, linking the cost directly to market rates on 24 September 2026, according to an <a href="https://x.com/FinMinNigeria/status/2103140179087073438/photo/1" target="_blank" rel="noopener">X </a>post.</p>
<p>The Nigeria Tax Administration (Interest on Late Payment of Tax) Order, 2026, takes effect on 1 October 2026 and applies across federal, state, and FCT tax authorities.</p>
<p>Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele issued the order under section 65 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025. The change connects late payment costs more closely to what the government pays when it borrows due to delayed tax collection.</p>
<p><strong>How the new rates work</strong></p>
<p>For taxes owed in Naira (NGN), the interest rate becomes the Central Bank of Nigeria&#8217;s Monetary Policy Rate plus 1 percentage point. However, the rate cannot fall below the yield on 364-day Treasury Bills. This represents a reduction from the previous 5-percentage-point spread.</p>
<p>For taxes owed in foreign currency, the rate is set at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) plus 6 percentage points. If SOFR is discontinued, its official successor rate applies.</p>
<p>The Nigeria Revenue Service calculates interest daily using simple interest from the due date until payment is made. The applicable rate changes once each month, with new figures published by the third business day of every month.</p>
<p><strong>What remains unchanged</strong></p>
<p>The 10% penalty for late payment under section 65 of the Act stays in place. Tax authorities retain the power under section 66 of the Act to waive penalties or interest if a taxpayer shows good cause.</p>
<p>The order affects all interest arising from 1 October 2026 onward, including interest on tax that came due before that date.</p>
<p>Earlier notices from 2017 and other prior guidance are superseded. Interest calculated under the old rules before 1 October is not affected.</p>

<p>Under Article 6 of the Personal Income Tax Law (GPMĮ), general annual aggregated income is taxed at 20% up to 36 average monthly wages (VDU), or EUR 83,237.40 for 2026. The rate is 25% between 36 and 60 VDU, or EUR 83,237.40 to EUR 138,729.00, and 32% above 60 VDU.</p>
<p>For individual activity, taxable income of up to EUR 20,000 is effectively taxed at 5% through the personal income tax credit. The effective rate rises gradually to 20% for taxable income up to EUR 42,500. Above EUR 42,500, the credit is zero and the whole amount is taxed under the general progressive rates.</p>
<p>The commentary also explains how different income categories are aggregated. Certain non-employment and individual activity income is taken into account before other income, such as employment income, when the progressive brackets are applied.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[France&#8217;s tax authorities issued ruling No. BOI-RES-TVA-000275 on 23 September 2026, confirming that intermediary transactions carried out by registered press-distribution intermediaries are excluded from the electronic invoicing obligation. Published by the French Directorate General of Public Finances, the ruling applies only to intermediation services covered by article 298 undecies of the CGI. Special VAT regime...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>France&#8217;s tax authorities issued <a href="https://bofip.impots.gouv.fr/bofip/15143-PGP.html/identifiant=BOI-RES-TVA-000275-20260923" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ruling No. BOI-RES-TVA-000275 on 23 September 2026</a>, confirming that intermediary transactions carried out by registered press-distribution intermediaries are excluded from the electronic invoicing obligation.</p>
<p>Published by the French Directorate General of Public Finances, the ruling applies only to intermediation services covered by article 298 undecies of the CGI.</p>
<p><strong>Special VAT regime for press intermediaries</strong></p>
<p>Under article 298 undecies, registered intermediaries distributing newspapers and periodicals benefit from a special VAT regime. Their intermediation services are exempt from VAT, while they keep full input VAT recovery rights. Press publishers, meanwhile, pay VAT on the total public retail price.</p>
<p><strong>Why the gap arose</strong></p>
<p>Under article 289 bis of the CGI, the statutory exemptions from e-invoicing cover only transactions exempted under articles 261 to 261 E of the CGI. Because article 298 undecies is not listed there, press intermediation was technically caught by the e-invoicing mandate, introduced in phases under article 26 of the Amended Finance Act for 2022.</p>
<p><strong>Operational concerns</strong></p>
<p>The authorities said imposing e-invoicing on these services would create significant operational burdens for the sector. Press distribution involves a structural separation between physical and financial flows among authorised distribution companies, depositaries and retailers. These services are not traditionally invoiced either; transactions are tracked through progress reports and current accounts (comptes rendus et comptes courants). The authorities noted that formal electronic invoices would bring no significant tax risk or yield.</p>
<p><strong>Nature of the exclusion and conditions</strong></p>
<p>The exclusion is an administrative tolerance, in place pending future legislative amendments that would extend the formal exemption. Intermediaries must maintain complete and strict documentary tracking through their existing reports and current account records.</p>
<p><strong>Limits of the tolerance</strong></p>
<p>The tolerance applies exclusively to article 298 undecies intermediation services. Press-distribution intermediaries and their principals must continue to comply with the mandatory e-invoicing rules for all other B2B transactions, whether they act as buyers, sellers or service providers.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bahrain&#8217;s National Bureau for Revenue (NBR) has issued revised editions of its <a href="https://www.nbr.gov.bh/publications/view/VAT_Registration_guide" target="_blank" rel="noopener">VAT Registration Guide </a>and<a href="https://www.nbr.gov.bh/publications/view/VAT_Deregistration_Manual" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> VAT Deregistration Manual</a>, dated 29 September 2026 and 28 September 2026 respectively.</p>
<p><strong>What the guides cover</strong></p>
<p>The VAT Registration Guide sets out the criteria and financial thresholds for mandatory and voluntary VAT registration, including requirements for non-residents and VAT groups. It also explains how to create an NBR profile and submit a registration application through the online portal.</p>
<p>The VAT Deregistration Manual explains when a business must or may cancel its VAT registration, the documents required and the online application process.</p>
<p><strong>Mandatory deregistration</strong></p>
<p>Resident taxable persons must deregister if they permanently cease economic activity, transfer or sell the business, or if the value of their taxable supplies falls below BHD 18,750 over 12 consecutive months and is not expected to exceed that level in the following 12 months.</p>
<p>Non-resident taxable persons must deregister if their standard-rated supplies to non-VAT-registered persons in Bahrain equal zero for 12 consecutive months.</p>
<p><strong>Voluntary deregistration</strong></p>
<p>Resident taxable persons whose annual taxable supplies fall below the mandatory threshold of BHD 37,500, but stay above BHD 18,750, may apply for voluntary deregistration.</p>
<p>Non-residents are not eligible. Taxable persons who registered voluntarily must remain registered for at least 24 months, and VAT group members must first exit their group.</p>
<p><strong>Grounds and application process</strong></p>
<p>Applications are made through the NBR portal and are based on the grounds in Article 34 of the VAT Law. These include cessation of economic activity and cessation of making taxable supplies for 12 consecutive months.</p>
<p>Applicants must upload supporting documents, such as proof of closure or transfer of the business, sales reports and expense forecasts. Audited financial statements or asset valuation reports may also be required.</p>
<p><strong>Finalisation and re-registration</strong></p>
<p>Deregistration is not finalised until all outstanding VAT returns are filed and all pending VAT liabilities or penalties are paid. If the NBR asks for more information, the applicant must respond within 30 calendar days or the request is cancelled automatically.</p>
<p>After approval, a Deregistration Confirmation Letter can be downloaded from the portal. A business that later meets or exceeds the mandatory registration threshold must re-register within 30 days.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dutch government published a <a href="https://open.overheid.nl/details/5d1a02b8-ff11-4b87-b6a4-bb0f9828eca0" target="_blank" rel="noopener">policy letter </a>from the State Secretary for Finance, Minister of Finance, and Prime Minister to the House of Representatives outlining key adjustments to the Tax Plan 2027 on individual taxation.</p>
<p>Key measures include accelerating the transition to a capital gains tax within box 3 by 2028, alongside a temporary reduction in the box 2 rate to encourage business investments and disincentivise excessive borrowing.</p>
<p><strong>Income tax &amp; purchasing power adjustments (Box 1)</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Higher top rate threshold: </strong>The income threshold above which the top tax rate applies is raised to EUR 80,578 (up from EUR 78,426).</li>
<li><strong>Rebalanced tax credits: </strong>Instead of providing additional relief through the employed person’s tax credit, which is set to increase by EUR 133 instead of EUR 173, the government will ease the phase-out of the general tax credit.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Substantial interest tax rate &amp; borrowing limits (Box 2)</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Temporary rate cut:</strong> The top bracket tax rate for Box 2 income (income from a substantial interest on amounts above EUR 68,843) is temporarily reduced by 1.8%, from 31% to 29.2%, for four years starting in 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Incentivising capital release:</strong> The temporary reduction is designed to encourage business owners to distribute locked-up capital from their companies at a lower rate, boosting short-term tax receipts for the state budget.</li>
<li><strong>Tightening excessive borrowing: </strong>Starting in 2027, the threshold for excessive borrowing from one&#8217;s own company will be gradually reduced to EUR 100,000 in five annual steps of EUR 80,000 (excluding loans taken out for a primary residence).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Box 3 reform: Shift to actual returns</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Legislative amendment: </strong>The government will submit a legislative amendment (novelle) to the Wet werkelijk rendement box 3 bill to accelerate the transition to taxation based on actual returns.</li>
<li><strong>2028 financial assets:</strong> From 2028, a capital gains tax will apply to financial assets, including stocks, bonds, and options, covering around 90% of Box 3 assets with value development.</li>
<li><strong>2030 full transition: </strong>By 2030, the capital gains tax system will be extended to all remaining Box 3 asset categories.</li>
<li><strong>2027 tax-free wealth allowance: </strong>The tax-free wealth allowance will be reduced to EUR 30,846 in 2027, returning to its 2020 level.</li>
<li><strong>2028 tax-free return allowance:</strong> A EUR 1,000 tax-free return allowance will be introduced from 2028. For example, a person holding EUR 50,000 earning 2% interest would have no taxable return.</li>
<li><strong>Higher deemed return rate:</strong> The higher deemed return rate for other assets, including real estate and rental income, will increase by 1.5 percentage points in 2027.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/netherlands-unveils-2027-tax-plan-with-corporate-vat-and-pit-changes/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, the Dutch government presented the 2027 Budget, including the Tax Plan for 2027, on 15 September 2026.</p>

The revised rules in Article 2 (paragraphs 2–11) and Article 4 (paragraphs 2–12) apply from 1 January 2028.</p>

Annual consumer price index adjustments to the non-taxable amount under Article 12a, paragraph 1, will begin in 2028.</p>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=89100</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The European Commission has published its October 2026 Infringements Package, which includes several tax-related infringement proceedings concerning EU Member States. Commission calls on Germany, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Hungary to enact effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties applicable to violations of rules set by the Directive on Administrative Cooperation in tax matters The European Commission has...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The European Commission has published its <a href="https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/inf_26_1760" target="_blank" rel="noopener">October 2026 Infringements Package</a>, which includes several tax-related infringement proceedings concerning EU Member States.</p>
<p><strong>Commission calls on Germany, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Hungary to enact effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties applicable to violations of rules set by the Directive on Administrative Cooperation in tax matters</strong></p>
<p>The European Commission has opened infringement procedures against Germany, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Hungary for failing to establish effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties for violations of the Directive on Administrative Cooperation in tax matters (DAC). The Commission considers the existing penalties too low to deter non-compliance and notes that the frameworks often do not adequately reflect the severity or repetition of violations, the offender’s financial capacity, or the economic incentives for non-compliance. The Commission has sent letters of formal notice, giving the five countries two months to respond; otherwise, it may issue reasoned opinions.</p>
<p><strong>Commission calls on Hungary to end discriminatory tax treatment of interest income on EU and EEA government bonds</strong></p>
<p>The Commission has opened an infringement procedure against Hungary over the tax treatment of government bond interest. Interest from qualifying Hungarian government bonds is exempt from income tax and social contribution tax, while comparable income from bonds issued or guaranteed by other EU Member States and EEA countries is taxed normally. The Commission considers this discriminatory treatment contrary to the free movement of capital under Article 63 TFEU and Article 40 of the EEA Agreement. Hungary has two months to respond before the Commission may issue a reasoned opinion.</p>
<p><strong>Commission calls on Romania to end discriminatory tax treatment of capital gains derived from the transfer of securities and other financial instruments where the financial intermediary is not established in Romania</strong></p>
<p>The Commission has opened an infringement procedure against Romania concerning higher tax rates on capital gains from securities and other financial instruments when the intermediary handling the transaction is established outside Romania. The Commission considers that this treatment makes services provided by financial intermediaries in other EU Member States and EEA countries less attractive and may breach the freedom to provide services under Article 56 TFEU and Article 36 of the EEA Agreement. Romania has two months to respond to the formal notice, after which a reasoned opinion may follow.</p>
<p><strong>Commission calls on Italy to end discriminatory tax treatment of interest and other income from Italian bonds for certain non-resident investors</strong></p>
<p>The Commission has opened an infringement procedure against Italy over conditions attached to tax exemptions on interest and other income from Italian government and corporate bonds. Certain non-resident investors can receive an exemption only where the bonds are held through an Italian-resident financial intermediary, an Italian permanent establishment, or, in some cases, a non-resident intermediary with an Italian tax representative. The Commission considers that these conditions disadvantage intermediaries established in other EU/EEA countries and may breach Article 56 TFEU and Article 36 of the EEA Agreement. Italy has two months to respond before a reasoned opinion may be issued.</p>
<p><strong>Commission calls on Ireland to end discriminatory tax treatment of capital gains on EU and EEA government bonds</strong></p>
<p>The Commission has opened an infringement procedure against Ireland concerning the tax treatment of capital gains from government bonds. Capital gains on bonds issued or guaranteed by the Irish Government and certain Irish governmental entities are exempt from capital gains tax, while gains on comparable bonds from other EU Member States and EEA countries are subject to the standard 33% capital gains tax rate. The Commission considers this difference inconsistent with the free movement of capital under Article 63 TFEU and Article 40 of the EEA Agreement. Ireland has two months to respond before the Commission may issue a reasoned opinion.</p>
<p><strong>Commission calls on Germany to correctly transpose and apply the VAT exemption for credit management and credit guarantee management services</strong></p>
<p>The Commission has opened an infringement procedure against Germany for failing to correctly transpose and apply the VAT exemption under Article 135(1)(b) and (c) of the VAT Directive for credit management and credit guarantee management services. The Commission considers that German VAT rules do not fully cover these services, resulting in VAT being charged on certain activities, including services provided by syndicate leaders in open syndicated loans, contrary to EU law. Germany has two months to respond before the Commission may issue a reasoned opinion.</p>
<p><strong>Commission calls on Czech Republic to finalise the implementation of the information exchange rules on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation (DAC9)</strong></p>
<p>The Commission has issued a reasoned opinion to the Czech Republic for failing to fully transpose Directive (EU) 2025/872, which amends the DAC rules on the collection and automatic exchange of top-up tax information returns under the Pillar 2 Directive. The Czech Republic has not yet adopted or notified all required national transposition measures, despite EU tax authorities being expected to exchange information on multinational groups within the Pillar 2 scope from June 2026. Czech Republic now has two months to comply; otherwise, the Commission may refer the case to the Court of Justice of the European Union and seek financial sanctions.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bulgaria&#8217;s Ministry of Finance opened a <a href="https://www.minfin.bg/bg/legislation7/624" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on 23 September 2026 on the Draft Law on Amendments to the Value Added Tax Law. The draft brings parts of the VAT in the Digital Age (ViDA) package, under Council Directive (EU) 2025/516, into national law and prepares VAT administration for the euro.</p>
<p>Most changes would apply from 1 January 2027. The e-invoicing rules, ledger repeal and pre-populated returns would start on 1 January 2028.</p>
<p><strong>E-invoicing</strong></p>
<p>Taxable persons established in Bulgaria would have to issue structured electronic invoices, credit notes and debit notes for domestic supplies to other taxable persons, legal non-taxable entities, and state or local government bodies (B2B and B2G transactions). The documents must follow Directive 2014/55/EU and the European e-invoicing standard.</p>
<p>The National Revenue Agency (NRA) will run a central information system. Invoices created in private software must be sent to it in real time. An e-invoice counts as issued only once the system generates a unique compliance code. The NRA must open a public testing environment six months before mandatory central reporting begins.</p>
<p><strong>Returns and ledgers</strong></p>
<p>The purchase and sales ledgers (дневник за покупки / продажби) will be abolished. By the second day after each tax period, the NRA will prepare a draft VAT declaration (справка-декларация) for each registered entity, using e-invoice and customs data. Taxpayers may adjust, add or delete entries before filing.</p>
<p><strong>Registration and input tax credit</strong></p>
<p>The VAT registration threshold will rise from 51,130 EUR to 75,000 EUR from 1 January 2027. Under Article 97g, registration will be compulsory for any taxable person, or physical person acting independently in an economic capacity, carrying out taxable transactions in new buildings, building land or construction rights (право на строеж). The application must be filed at least seven days before the tax point arises.</p>
<p>Input VAT must be claimed in the tax period when the right arose. A missed claim must be made by correcting that period&#8217;s declaration within 12 tax periods of the event. No deduction is allowed if the supplier failed to issue a required structured e-document.</p>
<p>Other measures</p>
<ul>
<li>Call-off stock: New arrangements will be banned after 30 June 2028, and the regime repealed after 30 June 2029.</li>
<li>One-Stop Shop (OSS): The scheme will be expanded to online platforms and electronic interfaces that facilitate sales of goods.</li>
<li>Defence products: A VAT zero rate (exemption with the right to deduct input tax) will apply from 1 January 2027 under Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1106 (the SAFE instrument).</li>
<li>Import scheme: The de minimis import scheme for investment projects will be removed from 1 January 2027.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Penalties</strong></p>
<p>Monetary penalties will be converted from BGN to EUR and revised for inflation and the euro, with amounts depending on the offender, from 1 January 2027. The new e-invoicing penalties are:</p>
<ul>
<li>Article 182a: Failure to issue a required structured e-invoice brings a fine equal to the uncharged tax. The minimum is 750 EUR for non-trader physical persons and 1,500 EUR for legal entities and sole proprietors. The penalty applies from 1 July 2028.</li>
<li>Article 192b: Software developers or distributors whose code errors block data transmission to the NRA face fines of 10,000 EUR to 20,000 EUR (physical persons) or 50,000 EUR to 100,000 EUR (legal entities). The fines double for repeat violations, and the software may be suspended temporarily.</li>
</ul>
<p>The public consultation on the draft will remain open for comments until 23 October 2026.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[Taiwan&#8217;s National Taxation Bureau of the Central Area, under the Ministry of Finance, has stated that where a decedent left a claim secured by a mortgage, the heirs should include the actual outstanding amount of that claim in the estate tax return, according to a release dated 30 September 2026. The Bureau explained that a...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan&#8217;s National Taxation Bureau of the Central Area, under the Ministry of Finance, has stated that where a decedent left a claim secured by a mortgage, the heirs should include the actual outstanding amount of that claim in the estate tax return, according to a release dated 30 September 2026.</p>
<p>The Bureau explained that a mortgage is a security interest over immovable property, provided by a debtor or a third party without transferring possession. If the secured claim is not repaid, the mortgagee may be satisfied from the proceeds of the sale of the mortgaged property. A mortgage is therefore a right in rem rather than a claim, and exists to secure a claim.</p>
<p>Accordingly, when calculating the value of an estate, Article 27 of the Enforcement Rules of the Estate and Gift Tax Act provides that the estate should be reported based on the amount of the claim. If interest has been agreed upon for the claim, the interest accrued up to the date of the decedent&#8217;s death should also be included.</p>
<p>Regardless of whether the right established by the decedent during their lifetime was an ordinary mortgage or a maximum amount mortgage, heirs should determine the amount to be reported based on the actual repayment received during the decedent&#8217;s lifetime. They should not simply report the &#8220;total amount of secured claims&#8221; stated in the mortgage registration section of the land registration transcript. Instead, the estate tax return should be based on the actual amount of the claim left by the decedent.</p>
<p>The Bureau also reminded taxpayers of a specific situation. If a mortgagee dies after the principal claim has been extinguished through repayment, but before the mortgage cancellation registration has been completed, the heirs should submit documentation proving repayment when filing the estate tax return. They should claim that the amount of the inherited claim was zero.</p>
<p>According to the Bureau, this can help avoid disputes between taxpayers and the tax authority at a later stage.</p>
<p>This <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/singlehtml/384fb3077bb349ea973e7fc6f13b6974?cntId=465183e8fa544a90822afd5d5e718ebd" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announcement</a> was made on 30 September 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Greece has postponed the start dates for mandatory electronic invoicing for businesses with turnover below EUR 1,000,000, as well as the deadlines for implementing Phase B of the digital monitoring of stock movements, according to joint decisions <a href="https://www.aade.gr/sites/default/files/2026-09/dt_30.09.2026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced </a>on 30 September 2026.</p>

<p><strong>Mandatory electronic invoicing for second-period businesses</strong></p>
<p>The postponement concerns businesses that declared gross revenue of up to and including EUR 1 million (EUR 1,000,000), based on the submitted return for the tax year that began within 2023.</p>

These are businesses with turnover below EUR 1,000,000 that issued or transmitted one invoice within 2025.</p>
<p>In the last month alone, almost 488,000 businesses submitted the relevant declaration or used an electronic invoicing provider or the AADE applications (timologio, myDATAapp). 										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The European Commission <a href="https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documents-register/detail?ref=C(2026)6694&amp;lang=en" target="_blank" rel="noopener">adopted</a> a Delegated Regulation on 21 September 2026 that introduces a fixed handling fee of EUR 2 per item. This charge applies to goods sold through distance sales by non-EU retailers and subsequently released for free circulation within the EU.</p>
<p>The regulation will become applicable across all Member States on 1 November 2026, ten days after publication in the Official Journal.</p>
<p>The new handling fee supplements Regulation (EU) 2026/2108, part of the broader<a href="https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/customs/eu-customs-reform_en" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> EU Customs Reform</a> that entered into force on 21 September 2026 with phased implementation through 2034. The measure aims to address rapid growth in low-value e-commerce shipments arriving at EU borders.</p>
<p><strong>What the fee covers</strong></p>
<p>The Commission calculated the EUR 2 amount to recover direct and indirect costs incurred by Member State customs authorities, the European Commission, and the EU Customs Authority. These covered operations include data verification and processing for distance sales transactions, risk analysis and security controls, physical and documentary checks, and post-release audits. The fee also accounts for maintenance of customs digital systems, staff dedicated to e-commerce clearance, and infrastructure services provided by the EU Customs Authority.</p>
<p>Historical volume data and projections for items valued at EUR 150 or less informed the cost calculation. However, the fee applies to all distance-sold items regardless of value. Costs funded solely by individual Member State budgets and routine checks by market surveillance authorities are excluded from the calculation.</p>
<p><strong>Separate from existing duties</strong></p>
<p>The EUR 2 handling fee operates independently of the temporary EUR 3 customs duty applied to items valued at EUR 150 or less. For goods meeting both criteria, both charges apply together upon release for free circulation.</p>
<p><strong>Adjustments and future changes</strong></p>
<p>The Commission will review the handling fee level every two years, beginning with the 2026 to 2028 cost report, to ensure it reflects actual operational expenses.</p>
<p>A different and reduced handling fee structure will take effect on 1 July 2028 for distance-sold goods placed in a customs warehouse before release into free circulation. The specific rate for warehouse-stored goods will be determined closer to the 2028 implementation date, as trade flows and supervisory costs may shift before that deadline.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/eu-parliament-approves-customs-reform-targeting-e-commerce-imports/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, the European Parliament approved a reform of the EU Customs Code on 16 September 2026, introducing a handling fee on e-commerce parcels shipped directly to EU consumers from non-EU web shops.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Trump administration has begun limiting aircraft component exports to China as part of a broader strategy to gain negotiating power over rare earth mineral access. <p><strong>Commerce Department takes action</strong></p>
<p>The Department of Commerce has slowed export licensing for airplane parts destined for China in recent weeks. Officials are also developing a new export rule that would make it simpler to restrict critical components like landing gear and aviation hydraulic fluid to Beijing.</p>

<p><strong>Earlier restrictions and recent developments</strong></p>
<p>The US imposed wider export controls on aircraft products in late spring 2025 as trade tensions intensified. Washington suspended licenses for GE Aerospace jet engines and Honeywell Aerospace navigation systems intended for COMAC. The administration also sent notifications to hydraulic fluid manufacturers that the product would fall under new export license requirements, though these restrictions proved temporary.</p>
<p><strong>Trade negotiations resume</strong></p>
<p>US and Chinese officials met in September 2026 in New York and Washington to address key economic matters between the nations, including rare earth mineral access, agricultural trade, and artificial intelligence regulation.</p>
<p>In early October 2026, the two countries <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-and-china-extend-trade-truce-push-for-bigger-agreement/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">extended their trade truce</a> from its original expiration date of 10 November 2026 to 10 January 2027. This provides negotiators additional time to resolve more complex trade issues.</p>
<p>The aerospace sector has largely avoided the widespread tariffs Trump&#8217;s administration imposed across other industries and trading partners.</p>
<p>However, the sector continues to experience supply chain disruptions tied to geopolitical tensions, particularly regarding Chinese controls on rare earth materials needed for thermal coating sprays used in jet engine protection.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/china-us-agree-to-broad-tariff-cuts-soybeans-remain-excluded/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, China and the US agreed to a reciprocal tariff reduction covering about USD 60 billion of goods, following their extension of the bilateral trade truce to 10 January 2027.</p>

<p>Two programmes drive this effort: the<a href="https://www.irs.gov/individuals/free-tax-return-preparation-for-qualifying-taxpayers" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) programme and the Tax Counselling for the Elderly (TCE) programme</a>. <p>The IRS stated that volunteers and community partners play an essential role in expanding access to free, trusted tax preparation services across the country. The agency provides comprehensive training for all volunteer positions, regardless of prior experience or background.</p>
<p><strong>Scale and reach in 2026</strong></p>
<p>During the 2026 tax year, the VITA and TCE programmes recorded significant participation. More than 84,500 volunteers helped taxpayers file nearly 2.9 million tax returns. Community organisations hosted approximately 9,000 VITA/TCE sites, including schools, nonprofits, financial institutions, faith-based groups and other local entities. These sites served seniors, taxpayers with disabilities and residents of rural communities.</p>
<p><strong>Flexible roles and opportunities</strong></p>
<p>The IRS offers volunteer positions suited to different skill levels, interests and time commitments. Many sites provide flexible hours and virtual options. Volunteers come from diverse backgrounds, including students, retirees and professionals.</p>
<p>Organisations interested in hosting a VITA/TCE site receive direct support from an IRS relationship manager who discusses implementation details and answers questions about programme requirements.</p>
<p><strong>How to participate</strong></p>
<p>Interested volunteers can submit the <a href="https://freetaxassistance.for.irs.gov/s/sign-up-form" target="_blank" rel="noopener">VITA/TCE sign-up form</a> available on IRS.gov. The IRS recommends submitting applications between October and January.</p>
<p>After submission, prospective volunteers receive a list of local VITA/TCE sites and an invitation to a virtual orientation within approximately 14 days. Additional programme details are available at the IRS Tax Volunteers section on IRS.gov.</p>

Legal foundation and scope The discretionary benchmark draws from several core laws: the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>China’s State Taxation Administration (STA) has released the National Tax Administrative Penalty Discretionary Benchmark (2026 Edition) through <a href="https://fgk.chinatax.gov.cn/zcfgk/c100012/c5252754/content.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Announcement No. 20 of 2026</a> on 28 September 2026. The new standards set uniform guidelines for how tax authorities impose administrative penalties across China&#8217;s regions.</p>
<p><strong>Legal foundation and scope</strong></p>
<p>The discretionary benchmark draws from several core laws: the Administrative Penalty Law, the Tax Collection Law and its implementing regulations, the Social Insurance Law, and the Measures for Invoice Administration. Tax authorities must now impose penalties within these standardised limits and must specify in their penalty decisions how the benchmark applies. Citing the benchmark alone is not a sufficient basis for a penalty decision.</p>
<p><strong>Rules for applying penalties</strong></p>
<p>Tax authorities follow the Rules for the Exercise of Discretionary Power in Tax Administrative Penalties, originally issued as Announcement No. 78 of 2016 and amended through Announcement No. 31 of 2018. Under these rules, three scenarios allow departures from standard penalties.</p>
<p>Minor violations listed in the official minor-items list can result in no penalty if the violation was corrected promptly and caused no harm. When legal grounds exist for leniency or mitigation, authorities must apply those reductions. Complex cases involving heavy penalties, widespread impact, or proposed penalty reductions go through collective deliberation before final decisions.</p>
<p><strong>Taxpayer protections</strong></p>
<p>Tax authorities must inform taxpayers of their rights to request recusal of officials, submit statements and defences, and demand hearings. These obligations apply whenever penalties are exercised.</p>
<p>The announcement takes effect on 1 November 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Brazilian Federal Revenue Service (RFB) <a href="https://www.gov.br/receitafederal/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/2026/outubro/receita-federal-atualiza-legislacao-do-adicional-da-csll-e-incorpora-nova-regra-simplificadora" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a>, on 1 October 2026, the publication of Normative Instruction RFB No. 2342 on 15 September 2026. The amendment introduces two main regulatory updates. The first establishes the Globe Simplifying Rule for Substance-Based Tax Incentives (RSGIF). The second extends the applicability period for the existing Globe Transition Simplifying Rule (RSGT).</p>
<p>The instruction amends RFB Instruction No. 2228/2024 to implement provisions from the OECD Inclusive Framework&#8217;s Side-by-Side Package, approved in January 2026. The changes align Brazil&#8217;s CSLL (Social Contribution on Net Profit) surcharge with international standards, as required by Law No. 15,079 of 3 October 2024.</p>
<p><strong>New substance-based tax incentive rule</strong></p>
<p>The RSGIF permits multinational corporate groups to classify qualified tax incentives as additions to Adjusted Covered Taxes. This treatment increases the effective tax rate and can reduce the Additional Social Contribution on Net Profit (AdCSLL) owed in a given jurisdiction.</p>
<p>A tax incentive qualifies as an IFQ (Qualified Tax Incentive) under this rule if it meets one of two conditions. First, the incentive must be linked to expenses the company incurs. Second, it must directly relate to production volume. In both cases, the incentive must reduce a tax liability that falls within the scope of Globe Rules.</p>
<p>The RFB specified that certain incentives do not qualify. These include incentives that reduce taxes outside the Globe Rules scope, those linked exclusively to already-excluded income, subsidies and general grants, incentives not available to all eligible companies, and those granted through government discretion rather than legal entitlement.</p>
<p>The amount added to Adjusted Covered Taxes cannot exceed the Substance Limit, which incorporates payroll and physical asset values in its calculation. Adoption of the RSGIF is optional and operates on a one-year election basis. The rule applies to fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Extended transition rule</strong></p>
<p>The amendment also extends the Globe Transition Simplifying Rule (RSGT) originally established in RFB Instruction No. 2228/2024. The extended rule now applies to fiscal years beginning on or before 31 December 2027, excluding fiscal years that end after 30 June 2029.</p>

The proposed 2027 budget aims to address a challenging economic backdrop characterised by a widened deficit of 5.4% of GDP in 2026 and mounting debt interest charges</p>
<p><strong>Corporate income tax (CIT) surcharge for large companies</strong></p>
<p>The budget includes a 30% reduction in the exceptional corporate income tax surcharge levied on large corporations.</p>
<p><strong>Specific surcharge for shipping companies under the tonnage tax regime</strong></p>
<p>The budget proposes targeted contributions from sectors benefiting from favourable economic conditions or windfall rents, while continuing structural support for shipowners and maritime activities. The executive summary does not provide details on the reintroduced tonnage tax surcharge for shipping companies with turnover of EUR 1 billion or more.</p>
<p><strong>Electronic invoicing</strong></p>
<p>The budget outlines the generalised rollout of mandatory electronic invoicing starting 1 January 2027, for all VAT-liable businesses to simplify reporting and strengthen anti-fraud controls.</p>
<p><strong>Business &amp; family transfers</strong></p>
<p>Rather than listing a general gift tax rate cut, the budget kit focuses on business transmission and intergenerational ownership transfers:</p>
<ul>
<li>Pacte Dutreil: Fully preserved without modifications to secure family business transfers.</li>
<li>Pacte Papin: Introduces new incentives to encourage employee buyouts when business owners retire, including additional capital gains tax allowances for retiring owners and reduced registration duties on transfers.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Extension of green industry tax credit (C3IV)</strong></p>
<p>The scope of the C3IV is expanded to cover investments in electrical power grids, solar thermal energy, battery packs for electric vehicles, and permanent magnets for electric propulsion.</p>
<p><strong>Industry 4.0 extraordinary tax deduction</strong></p>

<p><strong>Agricultural investment deduction</strong></p>
<p>A new special tax deduction supports investments labelled &#8220;future agricultural projects”.</p>
<p><strong>Local finance and green tax measures revised</strong></p>
<p>The 2027 budget reduces the standard VAT compensation rate for local authorities while introducing a 16.4% bonus rate for green transition and sustainable mobility investments. It also requires larger local authorities to contribute EUR 2.5 billion to fiscal consolidation, introduces a kerosene levy to support synthetic aviation fuel production, and revises older renewable energy contracts to reduce excessive rents.</p>
<p><strong>Adjustment of individual income tax brackets with inflation</strong></p>
<p>The budget confirms the indexation/revalorisation of the individual income tax scale in line with the annual inflation rate. This measure is designed to preserve household purchasing power and prevent &#8220;tax bracket creep,&#8221; protecting 20 million taxpaying households from an unlegislated tax increase caused solely by inflation.</p>
<p>The budget proposes indexing income tax brackets to inflation, noting that failure to do so could result in nearly 500,000 low-income households becoming liable for income tax for the first time. The general presentation does not specify the relevant legislative article number..</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Ukrainian Parliament is considering the <a href="https://itd.rada.gov.ua/billinfo/Bills/Card/70773" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft Law</a> on the State Budget for 2027, which was submitted on 15 September 2026. The draft sets a deficit limit of UAH 1.67 trillion and includes provisions for a fund to insure Ukrainian businesses against war risks, to be financed by an increase in value added tax (VAT).</p>
<p>Total revenues are projected at UAH 5.65 trillion, of which the General Fund accounts for UAH 3.22 trillion and the Special Fund for UAH 2.43 trillion. Total expenditures are set at UAH 7.27 trillion, split between the General Fund (UAH 4.78 trillion) and the Special Fund (UAH 2.49 trillion).</p>
<p>Loan repayments to the budget are projected at UAH 15.09 billion, while budget lending is set at UAH 57.26 billion. The deficit limit is UAH 1,666,129,359.9 thousand, comprising a General Fund deficit of UAH 1.57 trillion and a Special Fund deficit of UAH 95.29 billion.</p>
<p><strong>War risk insurance and VAT</strong></p>
<p>One of the main tax-related measures is the provision for establishing a fund to insure Ukrainian businesses against war risks. The fund would be financed by an increase in VAT. The change is expected to raise the standard VAT rate from 20% to 21%, which would require separate amendments to the Tax Code.</p>
<p><strong>Debt and guarantees</strong></p>
<p>The public debt limit as of 31 December 2027 is capped at UAH 12.31 trillion, and the state-guaranteed debt limit at UAH 382.24 billion. The Cabinet of Ministers may issue state guarantees of up to UAH 65 billion, including up to UAH 30 billion for defence and national security programmes. A further UAH 4.92 billion in guarantees may be issued under international agreements.</p>
<p><strong>Social standards and minimum wage</strong></p>
<p>From 1 January 2027, the average monthly subsistence minimum is set at UAH 3,559 per person. By category, it is:</p>
<ul>
<li>UAH 3,124 for children under six</li>
<li>UAH 3,895 for children aged six to 18</li>
<li>UAH 3,691 for able-bodied persons</li>
<li>UAH 2,878 for persons who have lost the ability to work</li>
</ul>
<p>The minimum wage is UAH 9,546 a month and UAH 57.50 an hour. Assistance to low-income families is pegged to the subsistence minimum at 60% for able-bodied persons, 100% for persons with disabilities or lost capacity, and 145% for children.</p>
<p><strong>Revenue mechanisms</strong></p>
<p>The National Bank of Ukraine must transfer at least UAH 48.7 billion of its distributable profit to the state budget. State-owned enterprises and joint-stock companies with state shares that do not approve dividends by 1 May must pay 90% of their net profit to the budget by 1 July. All military levy revenue collected in 2027 goes to the Special Fund to cover monetary compensation for Armed Forces personnel.</p>
<p>The budget also incorporates funds raised under international agreements, including the EU Support Loan agreement dated 27 May 2026. Repayment is tied to income generated from frozen Russian assets.</p>
<p><strong>Spending priorities</strong></p>
<p>Special revenues, including personal income tax redistributions from military personnel, are to be allocated as follows:</p>
<ul>
<li>60% to the Ministry of Defence, for defence-industrial reform, arms production, procurement and drone destruction incentives</li>
<li>30% to the State Special Communications Service</li>
<li>10% directly to military units for material and technical support</li>
</ul>
<p>Fines, confiscated assets and voluntary court settlements from investigations by the Bureau of Economic Security, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau, the State Bureau of Investigation and the State Audit Service are earmarked for procuring, repairing and modernising weapons.</p>
<p>The draft also creates the Fund for Liquidation of the Consequences of Armed Aggression within the Special Fund. It would finance economic, social and humanitarian recovery programmes, housing compensation for destroyed properties, and housing credit programmes for internally displaced persons and veterans. Road fund allocations are restructured to cover debt service on road construction loans and rules for local road subventions.</p>
