					<description><![CDATA[The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) updated its Transfer Pricing guidance page on 25 September 2026 with additional guidance on transfer pricing adjustments relating to share-based compensation. The update sets out a revised treatment for applying the arm&#8217;s length principle to share-based compensation. It takes effect from the Year of Assessment (YA) 2026. Under...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) updated its <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/specific-topics/transfer-pricing" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Transfer Pricing guidance</a> page on 25 September 2026 with additional guidance on transfer pricing adjustments relating to share-based compensation.</p>
<p>The update sets out a revised treatment for applying the arm&#8217;s length principle to share-based compensation. It takes effect from the Year of Assessment (YA) 2026. Under the revised treatment, employee stock option or compensation costs must be included in the cost base when taxpayers apply the full-cost mark-up under the Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM).</p>
<p>As a one-off measure, taxpayers may also apply the revised treatment to YA 2022 through YA 2025. The source text available for this report was cut off before the conditions for this option were stated, so taxpayers should check the IRAS page for the full terms.</p>
<p><strong>Arm&#8217;s length principle and three-step approach</strong></p>
<p>IRAS requires transactions between related parties to reflect pricing that independent entities would agree under comparable circumstances. These include the sale or purchase of goods, provision of services, transfer of intangibles, intercompany loans, and dealings between head offices and branches.</p>
<p>IRAS describes a three-step approach:</p>
<ul>
<li>Comparability analysis: identify comparable transactions or situations between unrelated parties.</li>
<li>Select the transfer pricing method and tested party: choose the most appropriate method and tested party.</li>
<li>Determine results: calculate the arm&#8217;s length outcome based on the analysis.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Adjustments and surcharge</strong></p>
<p>Where non-arm&#8217;s length pricing understates profits or overstates losses in Singapore, IRAS makes a transfer pricing adjustment under Section 34D of the Income Tax Act. A mandatory 5% surcharge applies to the amount of any transfer pricing adjustment from YA 2019, regardless of whether additional tax is payable.</p>
<p><strong>Documentation requirements</strong></p>
<p>Under Section 34F, taxpayers must prepare transfer pricing documentation (TPD) if gross trade or business revenue exceeds SGD 10 million for the basis period, or if TPD was required in the preceding basis period.</p>
<ul>
<li>TPD must be completed by the income tax return filing due date and retained for at least five years from the end of the basis period.</li>
<li>It does not have to be submitted with the tax return, but must be provided within 30 days of a request by IRAS.</li>
<li>Documentation may be refreshed once every three years using a simplified document, provided the underlying business facts and details remain accurate.</li>
<li>Failure to prepare, retain or submit TPD on time, or providing false or misleading documents, carries a fine of up to SGD 10,000 per offence.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Related party transaction reporting</strong></p>
<p>Companies must complete and submit the Form for Reporting Related Party Transactions (RPT) as part of Form C if the aggregate value of related party transactions disclosed in the financial statements exceeds SGD 15 million.</p>
<p><strong>Specific related party transactions</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Intra-group services: IRAS accepts a 5% cost mark-up for qualifying routine support services listed in its guidelines. It accepts a 5% profit mark-up under the OECD simplified approach for low value-adding intra-group services. Cost-pooling and pass-through arrangements are allowed with zero mark-up for pure cost-sharing arrangements or strict pass-through expenses, under specified conditions.</li>
<li>Domestic loans: For loans entered into on or after 1 January 2025 where neither party is in the lending business, taxpayers may apply the IRAS indicative margin or the arm&#8217;s length principle. IRAS will not make Section 34D adjustments for these loans.</li>
<li>Cross-border loans: These must follow the arm&#8217;s length principle. For loans not exceeding SGD 15 million, taxpayers may apply the IRAS published indicative margin over base rates, which is 1.80% over Risk-Free Rates for 2026.</li>
<li>Baseline marketing and distribution activities: IRAS is implementing the OECD Simplified and Streamlined Approach (SSA) on a pilot basis from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2028.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Dispute prevention and resolution</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers can manage transfer pricing risks and resolve double taxation issues through Advance Pricing Arrangements (APAs), Mutual Agreement Procedures (MAPs) and arbitration. Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) applies to eligible Singapore-headquartered multinational enterprise groups.</p>
<p>Taxpayers with share-based compensation arrangements will need to review their TNMM cost bases for YA 2026 onwards. They should also consider whether the one-off option for earlier years applies to them.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[Greece’s Independent Authority for Public Revenue (AADE) had issued Decision A. 1192/2026 on 22 September, 2026, setting out procedures and requirements for foreign pensioners transferring their tax residency to Greece under Article 5B of Law 4172/2013 (Income Tax Code). Published in FEK B&#8217; 5767/24.9.2026, the decision replaced Joint Ministerial Decision A. 1217/2020 and established the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Greece’s Independent Authority for Public Revenue (AADE) had issued <a href="https://aade.gr/sites/default/files/2026-09/a1192_2026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Decision A. 1192/2026</a> on 22 September, 2026, setting out procedures and requirements for foreign pensioners transferring their tax residency to Greece under Article 5B of Law 4172/2013 (Income Tax Code).</p>
<p>Published in FEK B&#8217; 5767/24.9.2026, the decision replaced Joint Ministerial Decision A. 1217/2020 and established the conditions for applying the special tax regime.</p>
<p><strong>Tax treatment</strong></p>
<p>Qualifying foreign-sourced income is subject to a 7% flat tax for up to 15 consecutive tax years, starting from the tax year in which the application is submitted. Payment of the tax exhausts Greek income tax obligations on the covered foreign-sourced income.</p>
<p>Foreign taxes paid on eligible income may be credited against the Greek 7% tax, subject to the applicable Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or, where no DTA exists, the relevant rules. Any excess foreign tax is not refundable.</p>
<p>Greek-sourced income, including real or imputed income, remains subject to the standard Greek income tax rates.</p>
<p><strong>Tax payment rules</strong></p>
<p>The annual 7% tax must be paid in one instalment by the last working day of December. The amount cannot be offset against other tax credits or paid under an instalment arrangement.</p>
<p>Failure to pay the full tax by the deadline automatically revokes the special regime for that tax year and subsequent years. The taxpayer then becomes subject to the standard worldwide income taxation rules in Greece.</p>
<p><strong>Eligibility requirements</strong></p>
<p>To qualify under Article 5B, an individual must:</p>
<ul>
<li>receive foreign pension income from mandatory public insurance, legally established occupational funds or group pension insurance policy payouts;</li>
<li>not have been a Greek tax resident for 5 out of the 6 years preceding the transfer of tax residency;</li>
<li>transfer tax residency from a state with an active agreement on international administrative tax cooperation with Greece; and</li>
<li>not simultaneously participate in the Article 5A non-dom investor regime.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Application procedure</strong></p>
<p>Applications are handled by KE.FO.D.E. Attica (Section A8&#8242;) or KE.FO.D.E. Thessaloniki (Section A5&#8242;), depending on the applicant’s jurisdiction.</p>
<p>Individuals transferring their tax residency on or before July 2 may apply in the year of arrival or the following year. Those transferring residency after July 2 may apply in the following tax year.</p>
<p>The application must be filed by October 31 of the relevant year. Supporting documents unavailable at the time of filing may be submitted by November 30 of the same tax year.</p>
<p>Applications and supporting documents may be submitted digitally through the myAADE portal using &#8220;Ta Aitimata mou&#8221;, by registered mail or courier, or in person by appointment through &#8220;Ta Rantevou mou&#8221;.</p>
<p>AADE must review applications and issue a decision within 60 days of filing and no later than the last working day of December.</p>
<p><strong>Required documents</strong></p>
<p>Applicants must provide official documentation from a foreign pension fund, public authority or insurance provider confirming payment of pension benefits.</p>
<p>Tax residency history may be verified automatically where AADE records establish foreign tax residency for 5 out of 6 preceding years, or where the individual is applying for a Greek Tax Identification Number (TIN) for the first time.</p>
<p>Where automatic verification is not possible, applicants must provide documents such as Tax Residence Certificates, official DTA application forms, foreign tax returns or assessments, or certifications from foreign authorities.</p>
<p>Foreign public documents generally require legalisation through an Apostille or consular certification and an official Greek translation, subject to specified exemptions.</p>
<p><strong>Revocation and family members</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers may voluntarily leave the regime by submitting a revocation request by October 31 of any tax year. After revocation, the taxpayer returns to the general tax rules and cannot re-apply under Article 5B.</p>
<p>The transfer of tax residency under Article 5B applies only to the applicant and does not automatically change the tax residency status of related family members.</p>
<p>This structure separates tax treatment, payment rules, eligibility, application procedure, documentation, and revocation, while keeping the legal terminology and details intact.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[Egypt’s Ministry of Finance (MoF) had published the 2026/2027 Citizen Budget on 19 September, outlining measures covering income tax, VAT, real estate tax, tax administration and customs. The package had focused on supporting healthcare, investment and business activity while encouraging tax compliance and simplifying administrative procedures. Income tax and investment incentives The Citizen Budget had...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Egypt’s Ministry of Finance (MoF) had published the <a href="https://mof.gov.eg/ar/posts/stateGeneralBudget/6aaac5d56440ca00082da26c/%D9%85%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%B2%D9%86%D8%A9%20%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%B7%D9%86%20%D9%84%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%85%20%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%8A%202026-2027" target="_blank" rel="noopener">2026/2027 Citizen Budget on 19 September</a>, outlining measures covering income tax, VAT, real estate tax, tax administration and customs. The package had focused on supporting healthcare, investment and business activity while encouraging tax compliance and simplifying administrative procedures.</p>
<p><strong>Income tax and investment incentives</strong></p>
<p>The Citizen Budget had proposed changes to the taxation of stock exchange transactions, including replacing capital gains tax on stock exchange trading with Stamp Duty.</p>
<p>For non-resident investors, the Stamp Duty rate had been reduced to 0.5 per thousand from 1.25 per thousand.</p>
<p>A three-year tax incentive had also been proposed to encourage companies to list on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX). For unlisted securities held for three years, an incentive equivalent to the Central Bank’s discount rate would be added to the acquisition cost when the securities were disposed of.</p>
<p>The measures had also addressed dividend taxation by providing for dividend distribution tax to be collected only once between holding and subsidiary companies resident in Egypt, preventing double taxation.</p>
<p>Companies contributing to national infrastructure projects had been eligible for additional incentives, including a higher approved deductible limit for debit interest on corporate loans and an exemption from foreign withholding tax on international loans and credit facilities.</p>
<p><strong>VAT measures</strong></p>
<p>The budget had reduced the VAT rate on medical devices and equipment to 5% from 14%. The measure had been intended to support the healthcare sector and align with the rollout of Phase 2 of the Universal Health Insurance System.</p>
<p>It had also provided full VAT exemptions for inputs used to manufacture kidney dialysis machines, dialysis filters, spare parts and related supplies, as well as inputs used to manufacture prosthetic devices, body implants and deficiency-compensating devices.</p>
<p>Services provided on goods in transit had also been exempted from VAT, covering transit trade and services performed on such goods.</p>
<p>In addition, companies providing non-banking financial services had been granted a full VAT exemption, regardless of their governing regulatory body. Financial services provided by the National Postal Authority (Egypt Post) had also been excluded from VAT.</p>
<p>The suspension of VAT payment on machinery and equipment used in industrial production, including medical machinery, equipment and devices, had been extended to four years from two years.</p>
<p>The measures had also provided for faster VAT refunds, including immediate refunds for compliant taxpayers included on a new White List.</p>
<p><strong>Tax refunds and simplified regime</strong></p>
<p>The budget had proposed reducing the refund period for tax credit balances older than three months for projects under the simplified tax regime to three months from six months. The refund period for other businesses had also been shortened to three months.</p>
<p>A temporary eight-month tax card had been proposed to facilitate and accelerate business incorporation and licensing.</p>
<p>The simplified flat-tax system for small businesses and taxpayers with annual turnover of up to EGP 20 million had been continued, with the government targeting the inclusion of 100,000 new taxpayers.</p>
<p><strong>Real estate tax measures</strong></p>
<p>Real estate disposal tax had remained at 2.5% of the property sale value for individuals, regardless of the frequency of transactions.</p>
<p>Transfers or disposals of property between spouses, parents, children and direct descendants had been granted a 100% exemption.</p>
<p>The payment period for real estate disposal tax had been extended to 60 days from the transaction date, compared with 30 days previously. A dedicated mobile application had also been planned for real estate disposal tax filings.</p>
<p>For property tax, the exemption threshold for a taxpayer’s primary residential unit had been raised to EGP 8 million from EGP 2 million.</p>
<p>The measures had also provided real estate tax relief where emergency circumstances or force majeure prevented an owner from using or benefiting from a property. The relief would apply from the date the event occurred rather than from the date an application was submitted.</p>
<p>Late-payment penalties had been capped so that total delay penalties could not exceed the principal tax debt. In disputed assessments, the tax payable would be calculated based on the Appeal Committee’s decision rather than the initial tax office assessment.</p>
<p><strong>Compliance and tax administration</strong></p>
<p>The budget had proposed a Tax Excellence Card for compliant taxpayers, providing priority services and administrative benefits.</p>
<p>A new White List had also been planned for compliant taxpayers eligible for expedited VAT refunds. In addition, three specialised high-service tax centres had been planned, including centres in New Cairo and New Alamein.</p>
<p>The measures had sought to facilitate the write-off of small uncollectible tax debts and reduce procedural burdens on financing firms.</p>
<p>The Tax Dispute Settlement Law had been renewed through December to allow taxpayers to voluntarily resolve outstanding tax disputes.</p>
<p>Egypt had also planned rules covering transfer pricing, international tax compliance, information exchange and preventing profit shifting. The electronic payroll system was to be expanded to cover all private sector companies.</p>
<p><strong>Customs reforms</strong></p>
<p>The Citizen Budget had also included measures to facilitate the clearance of transit shipments passing through Egyptian ports.</p>
<p>Exceptional customs clearance procedures would allow transit cargo to complete customs procedures without prior registration on the Advance Cargo Information (ACI) system.</p>
<p>The government had also planned a three-hub customs approach focused on simplification, strengthened oversight and reduced release times, in cooperation with the Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade.</p>
<p>The measures outlined in the 2026/2027 Citizen Budget had therefore covered tax relief, investment incentives, compliance initiatives and administrative reforms across Egypt’s tax and customs systems. The package had also placed emphasis on healthcare-related VAT relief, faster refunds, simplified procedures and improved customs clearance for transit trade.</p>

		<title>OECD urges stronger customs controls for EU CBAM</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/oecd-urges-stronger-customs-controls-for-eu-cbam/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=oecd-urges-stronger-customs-controls-for-eu-cbam</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Abdur Rouf]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 13:39:38 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Customs Duty]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[OECD]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=89022</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The OECD’s 2026 report, “Advancing the Implementation of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: Lessons from Romania” on 30 September 2026, provided practical guidance for National Competent Authorities (NCAs), Customs Authorities and other government agencies as the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) moved into its full operational phase. CBAM forms part of the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD’s 2026 report, “<a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/advancing-the-implementation-of-the-eu-carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism_3ff6655c-en/full-report/policy-and-economic-context_358f34f7.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advancing the Implementation of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: Lessons from Romania</a>” on 30 September 2026, provided practical guidance for National Competent Authorities (NCAs), Customs Authorities and other government agencies as the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) moved into its full operational phase.</p>
<p>CBAM forms part of the EU’s climate strategy under the European Green Deal and the Fit for 55 package. The mechanism is intended to address carbon leakage by applying a carbon price to selected imported goods corresponding to the carbon cost faced by domestic producers under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS).</p>
<p>The mechanism supports the EU’s objectives of reducing net greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by at least 55% by 2030 compared with 1990 levels and achieving climate neutrality by 2050.</p>
<p><strong>CBAM entered the definitive phase</strong></p>
<p>CBAM’s transitional period ran from 1 October 2023 to 31 December 2025, during which importers primarily had to report embedded emissions and provide data without financial obligations.</p>
<p>The definitive period started on 1 January 2026, introducing financial and compliance requirements for covered imports.</p>
<p>Importers of CBAM goods must obtain authorised CBAM declarant status. They are also required to submit annual CBAM declarations, have embedded emissions verified by third parties, and purchase and surrender CBAM certificates.</p>
<p>Each CBAM certificate represents one tonne of CO₂e of embedded emissions, with certificate prices linked to EU ETS allowance prices. The surrender requirement is being phased in alongside the progressive phase-out of free EU ETS allowance allocations for EU producers.</p>
<p>Importers can reduce their CBAM certificate obligations where an effective carbon price had already been paid in the country of origin for the emissions generated during production.</p>
<p><strong>Goods covered by CBAM</strong></p>
<p>CBAM applies to emissions-intensive products including iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen.</p>
<p>The mechanism also covers selected downstream products, including screws, bolts and structures, to reduce the risk of circumvention.</p>
<p>Certain imports are exempt, including goods below the annual 50-tonne de minimis threshold, military goods, certain waste and scrap, and goods originating in non-EU countries linked to the EU ETS.</p>
<p><strong>Role of national competent authorities</strong></p>
<p>The report had identified NCAs as having a central role in administering and enforcing CBAM.</p>
<p>NCAs assess applications for authorised CBAM declarant status, including applicants’ legal and financial stability. Entities established for less than two financial years are subject to financial guarantee requirements, which NCAs must monitor.</p>
<p>NCAs also oversee accredited verifiers, review annual CBAM declarations, manage CBAM certificate accounts and monitor compliance.</p>
<p>For authorised declarants that fail to surrender the required certificates by 30 September, the penalty is equal to the EU ETS excess emissions penalty of EUR 100/tCO₂e, adjusted for inflation.</p>
<p>Entities making unauthorised imports above the de minimis threshold face penalties ranging from three to five times the EU ETS rate.</p>
<p><strong>Customs Authorities to support border controls</strong></p>
<p>Customs Authorities have been assigned a key role in determining whether imported goods fall within CBAM’s scope and whether the de minimis threshold applies.</p>
<p>They must also verify importer authorisation through TARIC Y-codes and the CBAM Registry.</p>
<p>Customs declaration information, including EORI numbers, CN codes, mass, country of origin and CBAM Account Numbers, is collected and automatically transmitted to the European Commission through SURV3 and to NCAs.</p>
<p>The report also highlighted the need for Customs Authorities to address circumvention risks, including artificial shipment splitting, product misclassification and false origin documentation. Risk profiles for such activities can be incorporated into systems including CRMS2 and ICS2.</p>
<p><strong>Romania’s exposure to CBAM</strong></p>
<p>The report used Romania as a case study to demonstrate the economic and administrative implications of CBAM.</p>
<p>Romania’s production of CBAM goods, excluding electricity, amounted to EUR 4.4 billion in 2023, equivalent to about 1.4% of GDP and approximately 7% of industrial Gross Value Added.</p>
<p>Domestic CBAM production was concentrated mainly in iron and steel, cement and aluminium.</p>
<p>Romania imported EUR 11.5 billion of CBAM goods in 2024. Extra-EU countries accounted for 34% of total import value and 53% of total import quantity.</p>
<p>Among extra-EU imports, iron and steel accounted for 68% of value, followed by fertilisers at 12%, aluminium at 9% and electricity at 8%.</p>
<p>By sector, extra-EU sources accounted for the highest shares of Romania’s imports of cement at 82% and fertilisers at 62%.</p>
<p><strong>Turkey was leading extra-EU origin</strong></p>
<p>Türkiye was Romania’s largest extra-EU origin country for CBAM goods in 2024, with imports valued at EUR 1.6 billion, mainly comprising iron, steel and aluminium.</p>
<p>Other major non-EU origins included Serbia, China, Ukraine and Russia. Ukraine was particularly associated with cement imports, while Russia was a major source of fertilisers.</p>
<p>Romania also exported CBAM goods to extra-EU markets. Such exports totalled EUR 1.7 billion in 2024, representing about 25% of the country’s EUR 6.5 billion in total CBAM exports.</p>
<p>Iron and steel accounted for the largest share, with exports worth EUR 1.1 billion.</p>
<p><strong>OECD recommendations for national implementation</strong></p>
<p>The report had set out 21 recommendations for national authorities covering administrative capacity, authorisation, customs controls, enforcement and governance.</p>
<p>It called for authorities to establish compliance metrics, including measures comparing actual and default emissions and tracking reporting timeliness. It also recommended training officials in carbon accounting and trade rules.</p>
<p>For authorisation procedures, the report recommended automated tools for calculating financial guarantees and clear procedures for revoking authorised declarant status when non-compliance requirements are triggered.</p>
<p>Authorities were also encouraged to develop national penalty rulebooks in coordination with EU ETS teams to ensure consistent treatment of non-compliance and unauthorised imports.</p>
<p>On customs administration, the OECD recommended integrating automated CBAM checks into national customs clearance systems and ensuring interoperability with EU systems such as SURV3 and the CBAM Registry. National authorities were also advised to develop risk profiles targeting potential circumvention.</p>
<p>The report further recommended establishing a national CBAM Interministerial Working Group (IWG) and a Stakeholder Advisory Group. It called for national guidance handbooks and shared dashboards to support coordination and monitor implementation progress.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

<p>Key functions of the OECD Model Tax Convention include:</p>
<p><strong>Reducing double taxation: </strong>Establishes rules for allocating taxing rights between source and residence states and provides exemption or credit methods to relieve double taxation on cross-border income.</p>
<p><strong>Strengthening tax cooperation:</strong> Supports administrative cooperation through the exchange of information and assistance in the collection of taxes, while incorporating provisions to address tax avoidance and treaty abuse.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Kuwait’s Ministry of Finance (MoF) had <a href="https://www.mof.gov.kw/TCRS_Public/Content/MOF_user_manual_Public-v3.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">updated </a>its tax services portal on 28 September 2026 to allow multinational enterprise (MNE) groups registered for the Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (DMTT) to review and amend their registration applications. The update also requires all registered MNE groups to submit an update request, while enabling constituent entities (CEs) to obtain electronic tax cards with QR codes after approval.</p>
<p><strong>Amending the DMTT registration</strong></p>
<p>Under the updated procedure, the filing constituent entity (filing CE) may amend the DMTT registration application through its account on the portal. Amendments may cover:</p>
<ul>
<li>supporting documents;</li>
<li>fiscal year information;</li>
<li>financial data;</li>
<li>Central Bank of Kuwait exchange rates; and</li>
<li>other information previously submitted.</li>
</ul>
<p>Missing constituent entities (CEs) may be added, and entities that are no longer part of the MNE group may be removed.</p>
<p><strong>Who must act</strong></p>
<p>All registered MNE groups must submit an update request, even where no changes are required. Where the ultimate parent entity (UPE) is in Kuwait, it must act as the filing CE. Each CE must also hold a valid registration number under the DMTT registration framework.</p>
<p><strong>Electronic tax card</strong></p>
<p>Once the updated registration is approved, each CE must submit a separate tax card application through its own portal account. The tax card will be issued electronically with a QR code, replacing the manual issuance and signature process.</p>
<p><strong>DMTT registration in the user manual</strong></p>
<p>The Tax Services System User Manual (Version 4.0) lists the Supplementary Tax Registration for Multinational Enterprise Groups (DMTT / Pillar Two) as one of the portal&#8217;s core services. It is designed for MNE groups subject to Global Minimum Tax (Globe / DMTT) rules.</p>
<p>The registration collects details on the UPE, constituent entities, global consolidated financial data, Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) files and authorised local audit firms.</p>
<p><strong>Application process and documents</strong></p>
<p>Depending on the account type, applications follow a four-step or seven-step process. The steps cover primary information or tax details, address information, partner or shareholder details where foreign partners exist, document attachments, data confirmation, and declaration and submission. Applicants must tick the mandatory legal accuracy declarations before final submission, and they can save their progress and return later.</p>
<p>If a tax officer returns a request for modification or additional information, the user receives a system message with a &#8220;View&#8221; button to reopen, amend and resubmit it.</p>
<p>Supporting documents must be in PDF format, with a maximum size of 4 MB per file. Scans must be clear and legible, and multi-page documents must keep their page order.</p>
<p><strong>About the portal</strong></p>
<p>The portal forms part of the government&#8217;s digital transformation strategy. It replaces paper-based procedures with fully digital workflows, automated processing, and electronic notifications by email and SMS. It serves companies, professional and institutional entities, government entities and individuals operating in Kuwait.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Serbia’s Parliament has enacted the <a href="https://www.parlament.gov.rs/upload/archive/files/lat/pdf/zakoni/14_saziv/2547-26%20-%20Lat..pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Law on Amendments to the Law on Free Zones</a>, published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia No. 80/2026.</p>
<p>The Law entered into force on 8 September 2026.</p>
<p>The Law on Amendments to the Law on Free Zones introduces significant operational, procedural, and compliance updates for companies managing free zones and entities operating within them. Across the legislation, legal terminology is updated to align with broader customs regulations—for example, replacing the word &#8220;territory&#8221; with &#8220;customs territory&#8221; (carinsko područje) and updating &#8220;enterprises&#8221; to &#8220;legal entities&#8221; or &#8220;companies&#8221;.</p>
<p>The Act sets a transition period for certain tax exemptions, noting that specific provisions will expire at the start of 2032.</p>
<p>The key amendments are summarised below:</p>
<p><strong>Abolition of special import exemption regime (Effective 1 January 2032)</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Exemptions phased out:</strong> Articles 19–21 of the Law on Free Zones, along with Articles 5–6 of the amending Law, will cease to apply from 1 January 2032, ending the special duty exemptions for goods imported for business activities and facility construction in free zones.</li>
<li><strong>Transitional rule:</strong> Goods imported duty-free before 1 January 2032 will remain under customs supervision while the exemption conditions continue to be met.</li>
<li><strong>Post-2032 customs treatment:</strong> If a different customs treatment or use is approved after 1 January 2032, customs debt will be calculated and collected under the standard customs rules. Other general customs exemptions or reduced tariff rates remain available.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Handling foreign goods following termination of zone operations</strong></p>
<p>Once the operation period of a free zone expires, the zone user or customs procedure holder has two years to manage foreign goods intended for zone activities or facility construction.  During this period, they must request the customs authority to amend the special procedure authorisation, place the goods under another customs procedure, re-export them, or surrender or destroy them in accordance with the law.</p>
<p>If the goods are released into free circulation, customs duties and import charges are calculated based on the goods’ condition and the applicable rates on the date the customs declaration is accepted.</p>
<p><strong>Customs formalities and movement reporting</strong></p>
<p>Users of free zones must formally report the entry and removal of goods to the competent customs office. The amendments also require all customs formalities for bringing goods into, removing goods from, and storing goods in free zones to comply with the general customs regulations.</p>
<p><strong>Revised misdemeanour penalties</strong></p>
<p>Articles 13 and 14 amend Articles 34 and 35 of the Law on Free Zones to align fine amounts with the Misdemeanour Law, significantly increasing penalty ranges:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Zone management companies &amp; corporate users (legal entities):</strong> Minimum fines increase from RSD 10,000 to RSD 100,000, and maximum fines double from RSD 1,000,000 to RSD 2,000,000.</li>
<li><strong>Individual free zone users (sole proprietors/entrepreneurs):</strong> Minimum fines increase from RSD 500 to RSD 15,000, and maximum fines increase from RSD 50,000 to RSD 150,000.</li>
<li><strong>Responsible persons in legal entities &amp; management companies:</strong> Fines increase from RSD 500–50,000 to RSD 15,000 to RSD 150,000.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Administrative promotion rules</strong></p>
<p>The Free Zone Administration is tasked with promoting investment and business opportunities by collaborating broadly with competent authorities, institutions, and agencies (replacing older individual agency references such as SIEPA).</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Trump Administration is actively considering a diesel export ban as fuel prices continue climbing across the US. President Trump stated on 30 September 2026 that conversations about blocking diesel exports happen daily, with the administration scrambling to address soaring energy costs heading into the midterm elections.</p>
<p>Diesel prices reached USD 6.53 per gallon just a week before Trump&#8217;s announcement, according to AAA data. Gasoline prices have surged 40% over the past year. The price spikes stem from multiple disruptions: Iran&#8217;s war affecting supply, Ukraine&#8217;s attacks on Russian energy facilities cutting exports, and lost diesel shipments from the Middle East and China.</p>
<p>Trump acknowledged that a diesel export ban would hurt gasoline prices but could reduce diesel costs. The administration sees Russia&#8217;s invasion of Ukraine as the primary driver of the current crisis.</p>
<p>The Trump administration is exploring three main approaches: implementing a blanket ban on diesel exports, securing voluntary export limits from refiners, or expanding tax-exempt diesel sales. Energy Secretary Chris Wright confirmed that the Middle East and China have lost significant diesel export capacity, creating widespread interruptions across global markets.</p>
<p>The White House has also pushed the European Union to release emergency diesel stocks to stabilise prices and requested announcements from European officials about new diesel supply commitments.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/us-considers-fuel-tax-relief-as-diesel-prices-reach-record-highs/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, the Trump administration stated that it is considering expanding the use of red-dyed diesel to reduce fuel costs by allowing more buyers to avoid the federal diesel tax, while several states are pursuing separate measures to lower gasoline and diesel prices.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/tax-capacity-development-and-outreach.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">introduced</a> a new capacity-building programme on 22 September 2026 aimed at strengthening judges&#8217; expertise in international taxation across Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The initiative emerged from successful judicial training efforts in Ukraine and seeks to expand that model across the region through a train-the-trainer approach.</p>
<p><strong>Inaugural session draws over 100 judges</strong></p>
<p>The programme&#8217;s launch event brought together more than 100 judges from across 10 countries. Participants included judicial officials from Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Moldova, Mongolia, Ukraine, Uzbekistan, and Indonesia.</p>
<p><strong>What the first session covered</strong></p>
<p>Judges explored four core areas during the inaugural session. They examined the growing frequency of cross-border tax disputes in courtrooms and the practical challenges these cases present. The programme then addressed double taxation and double non-taxation problems, along with their impact on how courts resolve international tax cases.</p>
<p>Participants also reviewed the main sources of international tax law and tracked how international tax standards have evolved. The final component focused on the two foundational principles judges encounter: source-based taxation and residence-based taxation. Facilitators used real case examples to show how judges apply these concepts when deciding actual disputes.</p>
<p><strong>What comes next</strong></p>
<p>Coming sessions will advance into more complex international tax topics through expert instruction, case study reviews, and peer discussion among judges from different countries. The programme aims to create more consistent and informed judicial interpretations of international tax law across the region and improve how courts adjudicate cross-border tax disputes.</p>

These updates refine the legal framework governing electronic tax registration, VAT registration, reporting, and payment procedures for non-resident entities delivering e-commerce goods and services in Azerbaijan. The amendments also detail the administrative procedures, necessary documentation,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Azerbaijan Cabinet has issued <a href="https://nk.gov.az/az/senedler/qerarlar/azerbaycan-respublikasi-nazirler-kabinetinin-2023-9775" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Resolution No. 295 of 14 September 2026</a>, amending <a href="https://nk.gov.az/az/senedler/qerarlar/azerbaycan-respublikasi-nazirler-kabinetinin-2023-9775" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Resolution No. 387 of 30 October 2023</a>.</p>
<p>These updates refine the legal framework governing electronic tax registration, VAT registration, reporting, and payment procedures for non-resident entities delivering e-commerce goods and services in Azerbaijan. The amendments also detail the administrative procedures, necessary documentation, and conditions under which foreign digital service providers must fulfil their tax obligations.</p>
<p>The key structural changes introduced by Resolution No. 295 are summarised below:</p>
<p><strong>Shift in recipient scope (B2C focus vs. B2B reverse charge)</strong></p>
<p>Resolution No. 295 narrows the scope of the rules under Resolution No. 387 by replacing references to “residents” with “persons not registered with the tax authorities.” This change clarifies that the mandatory electronic tax registration, VAT registration, and direct VAT payment requirements for non-resident e-commerce businesses apply primarily to B2C transactions with unregistered end consumers.</p>
<p>Supplies made to tax-registered businesses or individuals are excluded from the direct non-resident filing and payment mechanism. Instead, VAT on these B2B transactions continues to be accounted for under the standard reverse-charge mechanism, with local tax agents responsible for the tax under Article 169 of the Tax Code.</p>
<p><strong>Statutory registration threshold</strong></p>
<p>Resolution No. 295 introduces an explicit USD 10,000 annual turnover threshold for electronic tax registration by non-residents providing electronic works and services to unregistered persons in Azerbaijan.</p>
<p>Non-residents must complete electronic tax registration within 30 days after their calendar-year turnover exceeds the threshold. Those whose annual turnover remains below USD 10,000 may register electronically voluntarily.</p>
<p><strong>Exclusions from e-commerce tax rules</strong></p>
<p>Resolution No. 295 adds Clause 1.4-1, clarifying that certain digital and online activities are excluded from the definition of e-commerce for tax registration and payment purposes.</p>
<p>The exclusions cover consulting, legal, financial, accounting, design, and engineering services provided by email or other interactive communication channels; teaching and training services delivered in real time via the Internet; and online reservations or bookings for tickets to scientific, educational, cultural, sports, and entertainment events.</p>
<p>Accordingly, these activities are excluded from the specific registration and VAT payment requirements applicable to non-resident e-commerce businesses.</p>
<p>The amendments generally take effect from 14 September 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD will hold a <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/events/public-consultations/2026/11/public-consultation-meeting-revisions-to-chapter-vii-of-the-oecd-transfer-pricing-guidelines.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> meeting on 9 November 2026 to discuss proposed revisions to Chapter VII of the <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-transfer-pricing-guidelines-for-multinational-enterprises-and-tax-administrations-2022_0e655865-en.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations</a>.</p>
<p>The meeting will focus on <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/events/public-consultations/2026/06/public-consultation-on-taxation-revisions-to-chapter-vii-of-the-oecd-transfer-pricing-guidelines.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">feedback</a> from a recent public consultation and will bring together stakeholders from various industries and regions to examine the proposed changes and their implications for the taxation of intra-group services.</p>
<p><strong>OECD updates transfer pricing guidance on intra-group services</strong></p>
<p>The OECD Committee on Fiscal Affairs is modernising Chapter VII of the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations. This chapter provides the framework for analysing intra-group services, which multinational enterprises commonly provide to affiliated companies within their corporate structure.</p>
<p>The revisions aim to align Chapter VII with the core principles outlined in Chapters I, II and III of the guidelines. The OECD is also adding new examples and clarifications to help tax authorities and businesses apply the rules more consistently. These changes maintain the existing transfer pricing principles and do not alter how intra-group services should be priced.</p>
<p><strong>Stakeholder input shapes final revisions</strong></p>
<p>The OECD sought broad feedback from different industries, regions and stakeholder groups on its proposed changes. In June 2026, the organisation released a discussion document for public consultation. Stakeholders submitted comments throughout the consultation period, and all feedback will inform the final recommendations.</p>
<p><strong>Meeting details</strong></p>
<p>The OECD will discuss the proposals and comments at a meeting on 9 November 2026. Attendance is available both virtually and in person, with registration closing on 15 October 2026.</p>
<p>Virtual registration opens through the OECD Zoom link, while in-person registration is handled through a separate form.</p>
<p>Space at the meeting venue is limited. If in-person requests exceed capacity, applicants will be offered remote participation instead. The OECD will send confirmation emails to all registered participants on 20 October 2026, including access details and venue information.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Kazakhstan&#8217;s Ministry of  Finance has released the draft Law &#8220;<a href="https://legalacts.egov.kz/npa/view?id=15900691" target="_blank" rel="noopener">On the Republican Budget for 2027–2029</a>,&#8221; establishing the government&#8217;s financial roadmap for the next three years. The budget does not introduce specific tax measures; it sets certain tax-related values, including the monthly calculation index (MCI) and the monthly minimum wage.</p>
<p>The legislation allocates KZT 29.02 trillion in spending and sets baseline rates for wages, pensions, and social benefits effective from 1 January 2027.</p>
<p>The budget plan targets a deficit of KZT 4.56 trillion, or 2.3% of GDP, while placing strict ceilings on government borrowing and debt accumulation. These fiscal parameters form the foundation for Kazakhstan&#8217;s monetary and social policy through 2029.</p>
<p><strong>Social and wage benchmarks</strong></p>

The minimum wage jumps to KZT 85,000 per month. The subsistence minimum is fixed at KZT 55,173 generally, with KZT 50,851 designated for calculating targeted social assistance.</p>
<p>Pension payments receive an uplift of 8.5% on the same date. The minimum base pension stands at KZT 38,622, while the floor for all pension payments reaches KZT 74,919 monthly.</p>
<p><strong>Revenue and spending</strong></p>
<p>The national budget projects total revenues of KZT 25.44 trillion, with tax collections accounting for KZT 19.54 trillion. Transfers contribute KZT 5.51 trillion, and non-tax income adds KZT 377.2 billion. Total expenditures are budgeted at KZT 29.02 trillion.</p>
<p>This spending plan produces a deficit of KZT 4.56 trillion, equivalent to 2.3% of gross domestic product. Excluding oil-related revenues, the non-oil deficit reaches KZT 10.62 trillion, or 5.3% of GDP.</p>
<p><strong>Fund transfers and regional distribution</strong></p>
<p>The National Fund transfers KZT 2.43 trillion as a guaranteed payment and allocates a further KZT 2.0 trillion for presidential priorities. Three donor regions remit funds to the central budget: Almaty City contributes KZT 600.9 billion, Astana City KZT 241.0 billion, and Atyrau Region KZT 237.9 billion.</p>
<p>Regional subventions total KZT 6.36 trillion, distributed to 17 regions and the city of Shymkent.</p>

<p><strong>VAT revenue and new beverage rates</strong></p>
<p>New VAT rates for specific beverage categories take effect on 1 January 2027, generating approximately PLN 1.3 billion in additional revenue while adjusting tax burdens in this sector. One offsetting factor is a VAT exemption for military equipment purchases financed through the SAFE instrument, which will reduce VAT revenue by approximately PLN 4.4 billion in 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Excise taxes rise on alcohol, tobacco, and vaping products</strong></p>
<p>Excise tax revenue reaches PLN 100.1 billion, up PLN 7.0 billion (7.5%) from 2026. Rate updates follow the government&#8217;s excise tax roadmap covering alcohol, tobacco, vaping products, electronic cigarette liquids, and nicotine sachets. Changes to taxation on vaping products and alcoholic beverages serve both revenue and public health goals aimed at reducing harm from these products.</p>
<p><strong>Personal income tax changes for the middle class</strong></p>
<p>The personal income tax brackets shift to reduce pressure on middle earners. The 12% tax rate threshold moves upward from PLN 120,000 to PLN 130,000. Income between PLN 130,000 and PLN 150,000 will face a new 24% rate, while the 32% rate applies to income above PLN 150,000.</p>
<p>A notable restriction targets high-income earners using simplified taxation on recorded revenues. The revenue ceiling for this option drops significantly from EUR 2 million to EUR 250,000. The government also introduced Personal Investment Accounts (OKI), a new savings and investment instrument that provides an alternative to current financial asset taxation methods.</p>

Under Paragraph 4, Category 5, Paragraph 1, Article 14 of...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan’s National Taxation Bureau of the Northern Area, Ministry of Finance, <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/singlehtml/384fb3077bb349ea973e7fc6f13b6974?cntId=236cbd307fff4d76a49f05aa3057b65c" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 30 September 2026 that individuals who provided houses they owned to companies for business use without charging rent were still required to calculate and report rental income for individual consolidated income tax.</p>
<p>Under Paragraph 4, Category 5, Paragraph 1, Article 14 of the Income Tax Act, when a taxpayer lends property to another person for use, rental income must be calculated based on prevailing local rental rates unless it is verified that the property was provided free of charge and was not used for business operations or the practice of a profession.</p>
<p>The bureau explained that Paragraph 2, Article 16 of the Enforcement Rules of the same Act defines “other persons” as individuals or juridical persons other than the taxpayer, the taxpayer’s spouse and lineal relatives. As a company is a “juridical person”, it is therefore regarded as an “other person” under the rules.</p>
<p>Accordingly, where a property is used for business purposes, rental income must be imputed and reported for individual consolidated income tax, regardless of whether the company was established by a relative or whether the property was provided free of charge.</p>
<p>The bureau gave the example of taxpayer Mr A, who in 2025 provided a house registered in his name free of charge to Company B, for which he was the responsible person, to register its business address and conduct business activities. Although Mr A did not collect rent, the company was a “juridical person” and the property was “used for business purposes”.</p>
<p>Based on prevailing local rental rates, the bureau calculated rental income for the year at TWD 120,000. After applying the 43% deduction, Mr A’s taxable rental income was TWD 64,000 [TWD 120,000 × (1 &#8211; 43%)], which was included in his individual consolidated income tax assessment.</p>
<p>As Company B had not actually paid rent, it could not report the imputed TWD 120,000 as rental expense when filing its profit-seeking enterprise income tax return for the year, under Subparagraph 7, Article 72 of the Regulations Governing the Assessment of Profit-Seeking Enterprise Income Tax.</p>
<p>The bureau reminded taxpayers who provide their property free of charge to companies or other persons for business operations or the practice of a profession to proactively report rental income based on prevailing local rental rates when filing their individual consolidated income tax returns. This would help avoid additional tax assessments arising from underreporting.</p>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=88946</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has updated its guidance on foreign currency transactions, adding sections on approved exchange rate sources, the treatment of different transaction types, and the reporting of exchange gains and losses. Invoicing requirements As reported in the guidance, for foreign currency sales, businesses must use approved GST exchange rates to...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has updated its guidance on <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/charging-gst-(output-tax)/foreign-currency-transactions" target="_blank" rel="noopener">foreign currency transactions</a>, adding sections on approved exchange rate sources, the treatment of different transaction types, and the reporting of exchange gains and losses.</p>
<p><strong>Invoicing requirements</strong></p>
<p>As reported in the guidance, for foreign currency sales, businesses must use approved <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/docs/default-source/e-tax/etaxguides_gst_exchange-rates-for-gst-purpose.pdf?sfvrsn=6746fd69_29" target="_blank" rel="noopener">GST exchange rates</a> to convert the amount excluding GST, GST payable, and total amount including GST into Singapore dollars. The Singapore dollar amounts may be shown alongside the foreign currency figures, and the selected exchange rate source must be updated at least every three months and used consistently for at least one year.</p>
<p><strong>Reporting requirements</strong></p>
<p>Businesses must report the Singapore dollar amounts stated on the tax invoice in their GST returns under Box 1: Total value of standard-rated supplies and Box 6: Output tax due.</p>
<p><strong>Purchases and imports denominated in foreign currency</strong></p>
<p>For foreign currency purchases, the supplier must state the GST payable on the tax invoice in Singapore dollars using the exchange rate from an approved source. Businesses must use this Singapore dollar amount when claiming input tax in their GST returns and should not use the amount recorded in their accounts if a different exchange rate was applied. For imports, input tax must be claimed based on the Singapore dollar amounts stated in the import permits issued by Singapore Customs.</p>
<p><strong>Preparations for foreign currency transactions</strong></p>
<p>Businesses should select an approved exchange rate source, establish systems to track exchange gains and losses, and ensure that their accounting systems can consistently convert foreign currency amounts.</p>
<p><strong>Approved exchange rate sources</strong></p>
<p>Approved exchange rate sources include Singapore banks, local newspapers, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). Global sources include reputable news agencies, eligible foreign central banks, and online platforms such as Yahoo! Finance and XE, provided their rates come from approved underlying sources.</p>
<p><strong>Treatment of different transaction types</strong></p>
<p>For sales, businesses must convert the total amount payable excluding GST, the GST amount, and the total amount payable including GST. These amounts are reported in Box 1: Standard-rated supplies and Box 6: Output tax.</p>
<p>For purchases, businesses should use the supplier’s Singapore dollar amounts stated on the tax invoice. For imports, they should use the Singapore dollar amounts stated on the relevant import permits. These amounts are reported in Box 5: Taxable purchases and Box 7: Input tax.</p>
<p><strong>Exchange gains and losses</strong></p>
<p>Exchange gains and losses from foreign currency transactions may constitute a GST supply. Realised gains and losses from completed transactions must be reported, while unrealised gains and losses are generally excluded unless an alternative reporting method is used. Year-end translation differences are not reported as they do not constitute a supply.</p>
<p>Businesses must calculate their net realised exchange gain or loss for each prescribed accounting period and report the absolute value in Box 3: Value of exempt supplies. For example, losses of SGD 150 and SGD 200, offset by a SGD 100 gain, produce a net loss of SGD 250, which is reported as SGD 250 in Box 3.</p>
<p><strong>Alternative reporting method</strong></p>
<p>Businesses that find it administratively difficult to distinguish between realised and unrealised exchange gains and losses may report the total value of both, provided that their accounting practices comply with proper accounting and reporting standards and they consistently use the same basis for reporting the value of exempt supplies arising from foreign currency and derivative transactions.</p>
<p>However, including unrealised gains and losses may affect input tax claims under the <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/claiming-gst-(input-tax)/claiming-input-tax-incurred-to-make-exempt-supplies" target="_blank" rel="noopener">De Minimis Rule</a>, so businesses should weigh the reduced tracking burden against the potential impact on their claims.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Trump administration is evaluating regulatory changes to lower fuel prices as diesel climbs to historic levels. The federal government is considering broader use of red-dyed diesel, which would allow more buyers to bypass the federal fuel tax on that fuel type.</p>
<p>Currently, highway diesel carries a 24.4-cent-per-gallon tax, while dyed diesel faces only a 0.1-cent-per-gallon charge from the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund.</p>
<p>Diesel hit a record USD 6.53 per gallon one week ago, according to AAA data, with national averages climbing above USD 6 per gallon. The price surge stems from global supply disruptions, including the US war on Iran and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, combined with dwindling international fuel reserves. Farm Belt lawmakers are pressing for action as farmers face steep fuel costs during harvest season.</p>
<p>The red-dyed diesel proposal emerged from administration discussions as an alternative to a full export ban on diesel, which President Trump has backed. However, the oil industry and wider business community have opposed an export ban.</p>
<p>Energy Secretary Chris Wright has been in talks with major refiners about voluntary export limits instead. A White House official stated that no final decisions have been made, but the president continues evaluating options.</p>
<p><strong>States act independently to ease fuel costs</strong></p>
<p>Several states have already implemented their own measures. Texas issued a statewide disaster declaration on Monday to expand dyed diesel use and lift weight restrictions on fuel and agricultural loads. Alabama, Louisiana, and Nebraska took similar steps to allow broader use of untaxed diesel or suspend penalties.</p>
<p>Georgia suspended its gasoline and diesel tax for 30 days and removed commercial vehicle weight restrictions. California lifted its seasonal summer-blend gasoline requirement and allowed winter-blend fuel immediately. Massachusetts plans to file legislation suspending its 24-cent-per-gallon tax on gasoline and diesel for two months, requiring retailers to pass savings to consumers.</p>
<p>Other states relaxed environmental rules. Michigan allowed winter-blend gasoline and E15 fuel sales through summer. Texas also suspended low-emission diesel regulations. Kentucky reduced its gasoline tax by 10 cents in May, while Indiana suspended sales tax on gasoline entirely.</p>
<p><strong>Industry sceptics question effectiveness</strong></p>
<p>Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, questioned whether red-dyed diesel expansion would meaningfully lower prices. Farmers already use untaxed dyed diesel, he noted, so allowing truckers the same access would mainly shift who pays taxes rather than increase overall supply or reduce prices.</p>
<p>The American Petroleum Institute, however, welcomed consideration of red-dyed diesel waivers as part of a broader effort to lower diesel costs.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) <a href="https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/treasury-irs-issue-proposed-regulations-on-installment-payments-for-tax-on-certain-farmland-sales" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced </a>on  28 September 2026 that it unveiled <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/2026-19888/election-to-pay-in-installments-tax-on-gain-from-certain-farmland-property" target="_blank" rel="noopener">proposed regulations</a> that allow sellers of qualifying farmland to spread their tax payments across four years instead of paying the full amount upfront.</p>
<p>Section 1062 of the Internal Revenue Code authorises this election for sales or exchanges of farmland that occur in tax years beginning after 4 July 2025. The measure aims to reduce the financial burden on farmers who sell their land to active farmers.</p>
<p>IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano stated that the regulations provide practical relief. &#8220;Farmers should have options when farmland is sold,&#8221; he said. &#8220;The Working Families Tax Cuts helps keep farmland in agricultural use by spreading tax payments over four years.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>What makes farmland eligible</strong></p>
<p>The farmland must meet several conditions. The property must be real property located in the United States. It must have been used for farming during substantially all of the 10 years before the sale, or leased to a qualified farmer for that purpose.</p>
<p>The buyer must be an individual actively engaged in farming. Additionally, the property must become subject to a legal restriction preventing non-agricultural use for 10 years after the sale.</p>
<p><strong>How the payment structure works</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers elect to pay 25% of their tax liability each year over four years. The first payment is due on the regular federal income tax return due date for the year of sale, without regard to filing extensions. Each remaining payment follows on the regular return due date of the following three tax years.</p>
<p><strong>Coverage for pass-through entities</strong></p>
<p>The proposed rules address sales by partnerships, S corporations, trusts, and estates. Partners and shareholders generally make their own elections regarding their share of the gain. When gain passes through a trust or estate to a beneficiary, similar rules apply.</p>
<p>The regulations also clarify how taxpayers satisfy the 10-year farming requirement when land is temporarily removed from production under government programs, when recognised farming practices require it, or when circumstances beyond the taxpayer&#8217;s control intervene.</p>

The guidelines detail the mandatory requirements, specific filing deadlines, Q&#38;As, examples for corporate taxpayers, and criteria for identifying related-party transactions, including exemptions for thresholds under EUR 90,000. 										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Latvia’s State Revenue Service (SRS) <a href="https://www.vid.gov.lv/lv/informativie-un-metodiskie-materiali-13" target="_blank" rel="noopener">updated</a> its corporate income tax guidance page on 18 September 2026 with new <a href="https://www.vid.gov.lv/lv/media/35667/download" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Guidelines on completing controlled transaction reports</a>.</p>
<p>The guidelines detail the mandatory requirements, specific filing deadlines, Q&amp;As, examples for corporate taxpayers, and criteria for identifying related-party transactions, including exemptions for thresholds under EUR 90,000. Furthermore, the document offers practical instructions on determining transaction values, handling Value Added Tax, and utilising specific classifications or the &#8220;Other&#8221; category when standard definitions are unavailable.</p>
<p>Latvia’s controlled transactions reporting requirement took effect on 1 January 2026 and applies to transactions in fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025.</p>
<p>Resident companies and non-resident permanent establishments subject to corporate income tax must file reports electronically through the SRS Electronic Declaration System (EDS), using the prescribed template or an XML file. The requirement covers transactions with related foreign entities or individuals and entities or persons in listed low-tax or no-tax jurisdictions.</p>
<p><strong>Reporting thresholds &amp; materiality rules</strong></p>
<p>Latvia requires controlled transaction reports when the total value of controlled transactions exceeds EUR 250,000 in a reporting fiscal year. Transactions with an individual partner of EUR 90,000 or less generally do not need to be reported. If each partner’s transactions remain within EUR 90,000, no report is required even when the overall threshold exceeds EUR 250,000. Reports must be filed electronically within 12 months after the end of the fiscal year.</p>
<p><strong>Content and structure of the report</strong></p>
<p>For each reportable controlled transaction, taxpayers must provide structured information on the transaction partner, transaction type and direction, and total amount. Amounts must be reported excluding VAT and based on the revenue or expenditure recorded in the accounts. The report must also detail the transfer pricing methodology, including the method used, comparable data source, tested party, market indicators, benchmark range or value, and the actual price, rate, or financial indicator applied.</p>
<p><strong>Practical guidance &amp; special reporting rules</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Transaction classification:</strong> Taxpayers should use the “Other” (Cits) classifier when predefined categories do not cover a transaction type or value indicator, such as share transfers or currency exchanges. A description of up to 50 characters must be provided, and the classifier should not be used as a general catch-all. The transaction’s economic substance must be clearly described.</li>
<li><strong>Transfer pricing methods:</strong> Reports may use only the five statutory transfer pricing methods prescribed under Latvian regulations. Where techniques such as Discounted Cash Flow (DCF), expert valuations, or combined methods are used, taxpayers must identify the primary underlying statutory method, typically the Comparable Uncontrolled Price method.</li>
<li><strong>Grouping of transactions:</strong> Homogeneous transactions involving the same partner and direction may be aggregated into one entry, such as recurring management fees or freight forwarding invoices. However, transactions with opposite directions, such as purchases and sales, cannot be netted and must be reported separately.</li>
<li><strong>Portfolio approach: </strong>Where multiple partners have the same functional profile and are assessed using the same benchmark, each partner must still be reported separately. The relevant indicator ranges should remain consistent where the same benchmark is applied.</li>
<li><strong>Financial transactions: F</strong>or variable-rate loans, such as EURIBOR plus a margin, the report should include the total effective interest rate at commencement. For multiple financial transactions with different rates, taxpayers may report an arithmetic average rate, while providing the detailed rates and supporting information in the local transfer pricing documentation.</li>
<li><strong>Third-party cost recharges:</strong> Third-party cost recharges should be classified using “External comparable data”, with the applicable profit markup reported as 0, or as a 0 to 0 range.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Domestic chain transactions, documentation &amp; penalties</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Domestic chain transactions excluded: </strong>Domestic chain transactions (transactions with a related resident linked to a related foreign entity within a single supply chain) are not reported in the Controlled Transactions Report.</li>
<li><strong>Alignment with local file:</strong> Information submitted in the report must strictly reconcile with accounting records and local transfer pricing documentation.</li>
<li><strong>Penalties for non-compliance:</strong> Late submission or failure to provide essential information preventing arm&#8217;s-length verification can incur fines of up to 1% of the controlled transaction value, capped at EUR 100,000.</li>
</ul>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic had opened a <a href="https://www.consultoria.gov.do/consultas/publicas/consulta-publica-borrador-de-reglamento-sobre-regimen-simplificado-de-tributacion-rst-9756" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on a draft Regulation governing the Simplified Taxation Regime (RST), with the consultation beginning on 21 September 2026. The proposed regulation would update the regime for small taxpayers and incorporate amendments introduced to the Tax Code by Law No. 30-26.</p>
<p><strong>Scope of the RST</strong></p>
<p>The draft would cover both Income Tax (ISR) and ITBIS and would establish two modalities: RST by Income and RST by Purchases.</p>
<p>RST by Income would apply to individuals earning professional, independent trade or employment income, legal entities engaged in services or the production of goods, and agricultural producers. The annual income threshold would be DOP 30 million for legal entities and DOP 15 million for individuals and agricultural taxpayers.</p>
<p>RST by Purchases would apply to individuals or legal entities exclusively engaged in trading goods, with annual purchases and imports of up to DOP 60 million. The thresholds would be adjusted annually for inflation by the DGII.</p>
<p><strong>Entry and compliance requirements</strong></p>
<p>The draft would set requirements for entering and remaining in the RST, including registration and updating in the RNC, a 31 December fiscal year-end and compliance with tax obligations.</p>
<p>Certain activities would be excluded, including real estate construction, insurance, telecommunications, finance, pensions, the securities market, manufacturing of certain products subject to selective taxes, regular vehicle sales and activities involving precious metals.</p>
<p>The proposal would also impose corporate restrictions and exclude cases involving the concealment or simulation of income, purchases or imports.</p>
<p>RST taxpayers would be exempt from certain obligations under the ordinary regime, including Income Tax advance payments, the Asset Tax and certain information returns. They would nevertheless be required to issue tax receipts, request invoices from suppliers, identify themselves as RST taxpayers, register for electronic invoicing and retain supporting documentation.</p>
<p>Where taxpayers under the ordinary regime, state institutions or non-profit entities purchase goods or services from RST taxpayers, the draft would require withholding of 100% of the ITBIS invoiced, subject to applicable exceptions.</p>
<p>Applications to enter the regime would be submitted to the DGII, which would have 15 business days to make a decision.</p>
<p><strong>Tax rates</strong></p>
<p>For legal entities under RST by Income, the draft would establish a progressive Effective Tax Rate (TET) combining ISR and ITBIS. The rates would be 7%, 9% on the excess in the second bracket and 11% on the excess in the highest bracket, according to the prescribed income levels.</p>
<p>For individuals, ISR would be calculated based on taxable net income. Taxpayers would be permitted to deduct 40% of income from economic or professional activities, in addition to the personal exemption and allowable educational expenses.</p>
<p>A Basic RST would also cover small-scale economic activities with annual income below DOP 1 million, applying a fixed TET of 3% on gross income. Eligible activities would include trades, artisanal activities, small services and basic retail trade.</p>
<p>Agricultural taxpayers would be subject to a TET of 1.5% on annual gross income.</p>
<p>Under RST by Purchases, tax would be calculated using a TET of 4.5% applied to estimated annual income, based on the relevant purchases, imports and commercialisation margins.</p>
<p><strong>Filing and exclusion</strong></p>
<p>Tax returns would be filed annually. Individuals, agricultural taxpayers and Basic RST taxpayers would pay in two instalments, while legal entities and RST by Purchases taxpayers would make four quarterly payments.</p>
<p>The DGII could exclude taxpayers ex officio for non-compliance, obstruction of tax audits, loss of eligibility, exceeding applicable thresholds or detected irregularities. Taxpayers would be able to request a review and retain the administrative or judicial remedies available under the law.</p>
<p>The proposed regulation would apply from fiscal year 2026 and provide for the automatic migration of taxpayers already covered by the previous regime. It would also repeal and replace Decree No. 265-19.</p>
<p>The public consultation would remain open until 25 November 2026, with questions and comments to be submitted through the “submit comments” form accompanying the publication.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Thailand’s Excise Department has announced a public hearing for a new regulation that changes how export taxes work for tobacco products.</p>
<p>Under the current system, companies get immediate tax exemptions for goods destined for foreign markets. The new rule replaces this with a stricter model: exporters pay the excise tax upfront, then receive refunds once the shipment is verified as actually leaving the country.</p>
<p><strong>From exemption to verification</strong></p>
<p>The regulation stems from Section 103 of the Excise Tax Act B.E. 2560 and introduces a &#8220;pay-first, refund-later&#8221; approach. This shift addresses a persistent problem. The existing system relies on package markings that read &#8220;FOR EXPORT ONLY,&#8221; but these labels have failed to stop tobacco from being smuggled back into Thailand&#8217;s domestic market. By requiring upfront payment followed by verification, the department gains a clearer window to confirm actual exportation before granting any tax relief.</p>
<p><strong>What this means for industry</strong></p>
<p>For tobacco operators and importers, the change creates both constraints and clarity. Cash flow becomes tighter in the short term since taxes must be paid before shipment. However, companies gain operational simplicity by avoiding the requirement to affix physical excise stamps on export packages. This trade-off delivers more legal certainty around compliance standards and reduces confusion about what qualifies as a legitimate export transaction.</p>
<p><strong>Government priorities</strong></p>
<p>The department sees the regulation as a tool to combat tax evasion. By establishing strict verification procedures, officials can track shipments more effectively and reduce the volume of smuggled goods re-entering domestic channels. The framework gives revenue officers a definitive checklist for shipment approval rather than relying on marking systems that have proven ineffective. This shift strengthens the state&#8217;s ability to collect taxes fairly and ensures that domestic competitors face consistent regulatory treatment.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Polish Council of Ministers <a href="https://www.gov.pl/web/finanse/rada-ministrow-przyjela-pakiet-zmian-podatkowych-nizsze-podatki-dla-klasy-sredniej-wsparcie-robotyzacji-i-uszczelnienie-systemu" target="_blank" rel="noopener">adopted</a> a comprehensive tax reform package on 29 September 2026, designed to ease the tax burden on roughly 3.5 million middle-income earners while increasing contributions from high earners and large corporations. The changes take effect on 1 January 2027.</p>
<p><strong>New tax brackets reshape personal income</strong></p>
<p>Poland&#8217;s personal income tax system will shift to a three-tiered structure. The first threshold rises from PLN 120,000 to PLN 130,000 annually, with a new 24% rate applied to income between PLN 130,000 and PLN 150,000. Income exceeding PLN 150,000 faces a 32% rate. The government designed these changes to prevent sharp tax jumps for wage earners, self-employed workers, and pensioners who cross threshold limits.</p>
<p>At the top end, the solidarity levy increases from 4% to 5% for annual income exceeding PLN 1 million. Companies generating revenues over €50 million annually will pay corporate income tax at 22%, up from the current 19% standard rate.</p>
<p><strong>Tighter rules for small business and family structures</strong></p>
<p>The flat-rate tax threshold for small business owners drops from EUR 2 million to EUR 250,000 in revenue, narrowing access to simplified taxation designed for genuinely small enterprises. The government views the previous limit as too generous.</p>
<p>Family foundations face stricter requirements. They must now hold assets for at least two years to receive preferential tax treatment. The tax rate for certain transactions rises from 15% to 19%.</p>
<p>New provisions treat family foundations like controlled foreign entities and restrict business conducted through tax-transparent structures. The rules also extend inheritance tax exemptions to stepchildren and descendants of founders&#8217; siblings, supporting multigenerational business succession.</p>
<p><strong>Incentives and eliminations</strong></p>
<p>The government will extend the robotisation tax relief for 10 years, allowing businesses to deduct up to 50% of eligible robotic production investment costs from their tax base. The measure aims to support business modernisation, productivity, and competitiveness while clarifying existing rules to improve legal certainty for businesses.</p>
<p>The government eliminated the internet tax credit, concluding it no longer serves a purpose now that internet access is widespread. Tax relief for business expansion activities also ends, as analyses showed it rarely generated the projected economic gains.</p>
