		<category><![CDATA[WTO]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=88145</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The World Trade Organisation (WTO) has published its World Trade Report 2026: A Critical Juncture for the World Trading System on 15 September 2026, examining the multilateral trading system at a critical juncture, where the WTO must adapt to a modern, multipolar global economy. The report outlines how the system’s past successes in fostering openness...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The World Trade Organisation (WTO) has <a href="https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/publications_e/world-trade-report-2026_execsum_e.htm" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> its <a href="https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/wtr26_e.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">World Trade Report 2026: A Critical Juncture for the World Trading System</a> on 15 September 2026, examining the multilateral trading system at a critical juncture, where the WTO must adapt to a modern, multipolar global economy. The report outlines how the system’s past successes in fostering openness and integration have created new complexities, such as shifting economic power and the rise of digital trade.</p>
<p>The World Trade Report 2026 also steps back to conduct a foundational assessment of the 80-year multilateral trading system. It details how reciprocal market opening under GATT and the WTO created an unprecedented level of global economic integration, while examining why modern structural transformations—such as shifting economic power, expanded state intervention, digitalisation, climate policies, and geopolitical rivalry—are placing the system under severe strain.</p>
<p><strong>The decline of tariffs and the shift toward non-tariff measures</strong></p>
<p>The report highlights the historic achievement of the multilateral trading system in reducing border barriers and establishing predictable rules:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Substantial tariff reductions: </strong>Average industrial tariffs among major economies dropped from 20%–25% before the first GATT Round in 1947 to approximately 3% by the creation of the WTO in 1995. For economies acceding to the WTO post-1995, average tariffs fell from 10.5% pre-accession to 7%.</li>
<li><strong>MFN baseline: </strong>Despite recent unilateral trade actions, approximately 72% of global merchandise trade continues to take place on Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) tariff terms committed to by WTO members.</li>
<li><strong>Tariff bindings &amp; predictability:</strong> Legal tariff ceilings (&#8220;tariff bindings&#8221;) significantly reduced trade policy uncertainty. During the Uruguay Round, the share of bound industrial tariff lines expanded from 78% to 99% in developed economies and from 21% to 73% in developing economies, while agricultural bindings reached 100%.</li>
<li><strong>Evolving cost structure: </strong>Because border tariffs have fallen so low, tariffs accounted for only about 14% of trade policy-related trade costs for goods in 2022. Non-tariff measures (NTMs), administrative frictions, and regulatory divergence now represent a far greater share of global trade costs.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Environmental policy, carbon pricing, and WTO rules</strong></p>
<p>The report emphasises that environmental policies have moved to the centre of global trade governance:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Carbon pricing&#8217;s rapid expansion: </strong>Carbon pricing has gone from a footnote to a mainstream policy tool in three decades. In 1995, it touched just 0.7% of global greenhouse gas emissions; by 2025 that figure sits at 28%.</li>
<li><strong>WTO notifications track the shift: </strong>The WTO has watched this shift closely — members filed over 7,000 climate-related trade notifications between 2009 and 2024, covering everything from subsidies to import restrictions to technical regulations.</li>
<li><strong>The leakage problem:</strong> The economic logic behind carbon taxes and emissions trading schemes is straightforward: they&#8217;re the cheapest way to cut emissions per ton. But run them unevenly across countries, and you get a problem. Higher domestic carbon costs push production toward places with looser rules, which is carbon leakage in practice, not theory. That&#8217;s the reasoning behind border carbon adjustment mechanisms like the EU&#8217;s CBAM: tax imports at the border to match what domestic producers already pay.</li>
<li><strong>The legal backstop: </strong>GATT Article XX: GATT Article XX gives WTO members room to run environmental policy even when it affects trade, as long as the measure isn&#8217;t a smokescreen for protectionism or arbitrary discrimination. That clause is doing a lot of work right now, since almost every new carbon border measure will eventually get tested against it.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Four core developments testing the multilateral system</strong></p>
<p>The report identifies four major structural shifts that are straining the existing WTO rulebook:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Shift in global economic power:</strong> Low- and middle-income economies nearly doubled their share of global trade, from 23% in 1995 to 45% in 2024. But the rulebook hasn&#8217;t caught up: market access commitments are still tethered to bindings negotiated during the Uruguay Round decades ago. That&#8217;s a straight mismatch between who holds market power today and which legal rules were built for a different distribution of it.</li>
<li><strong>Industrial policy and government intervention:</strong> Subsidies, state-owned enterprises, and industrial strategy have surged back into fashion, and that&#8217;s reopened old fights about a level playing field between fundamentally different economic models. Transparency hasn&#8217;t kept pace with the spending. Between 2015 and 2024, only 59% of WTO members submitted their mandatory subsidy notifications, and 77% of those came in late.</li>
<li><strong>The changing nature of trade:</strong> Global value chains accounted for 46% of global trade in 2024. Digitally delivered services grew more than fivefold between 2005 and 2025, now making up 55% of global services exports. Trade friction has followed that shift: it&#8217;s moved off the border and into domestic regulation and data governance, areas tariffs were never designed to touch.</li>
<li><strong>Geopolitical tensions and security:</strong> Rising geopolitical distance, chokepoints in critical minerals and semiconductors, and the spread of dual-use technologies have pushed governments to treat trade interdependence itself as a security risk rather than an economic asset.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Economic consequences of multilateral fragmentation</strong></p>
<p>The WTO’s modelling suggests that a breakdown of the multilateral rules-based trading system could reduce global GDP by 5%–10% by 2050, with smaller, lower-income, and developing economies facing disproportionately larger losses in GDP and trade than high-income economies.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) <a href="https://www.zra.org.zm/suspension-of-import-duty-on-wheat/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 11 September 2026 that the Government had temporarily suspended customs duty on specified wheat imports under Statutory Instrument No. 65 of 2026.</p>
<p>The measure was provided for under the Customs and Excise (Suspension) (Wheat) (No. 2) Regulations, 2026 and was deemed to have taken effect on 1 September 2026. The Regulations will remain in force until 30 September 2026, when they will be revoked.</p>
<p>Under the Regulations, customs duty on wheat classified under tariff headings 1001.19.00 and 1001.91.90 had been suspended to zero percent, subject to the conditions set out in the Statutory Instrument.</p>
<p>The suspension applied where the wheat was imported by a holder of a valid import permit issued by the Ministry responsible for Agriculture, the importer was one of the companies specified in the Schedule to the Regulations, and the quantities imported were within the respective approved quantities in the Schedule.</p>
<p>The Statutory Instrument covered a combined 300,000 metric tonnes of wheat allocated among 26 specified companies.</p>
<p>ZRA clarified that the measure was not a general duty waiver for all wheat importers. Only imports meeting the requirements of Statutory Instrument No. 65 of 2026 would qualify for the zero rate of customs duty during the prescribed period.</p>
<p>Importers and clearing agents were required to present supporting documentation, including the relevant import permit, at customs clearance to facilitate processing.</p>
<p>Eligible importers were also advised to monitor their approved quantities and complete imports within the period provided under the Regulations.</p>

The draft law, Ref. No. 52-654-01-132, was submitted on 10 September 2026 by Members...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bulgaria&#8217;s National Assembly (parliament) is considering a Draft Law on Amendments and Supplements to the Corporate Income Taxation Act, which is meant to stimulate economic growth and industrial production by encouraging businesses to reinvest their profits into machinery and production equipment.</p>
<p>The draft law, <a href="https://www.parliament.bg/bg/bills/ID/167541" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Ref. No. 52-654-01-132, was submitted on 10 September 2026 </a>by Members of Parliament including Martin Dimitrov, Bozhidar Bozhanov, Ivaylo Mirchev, Atanas Slavov and Elisaveta Belobradova, among others.</p>
<p>Under the proposal, the maximum annual tax depreciation rate for Category II assets, covering machinery, production equipment and apparatus, would increase from 30% to 100%.</p>
<p>The maximum rate for Category IV assets, covering computers, peripheral equipment and software, would also increase from 50% to 100%.</p>
<p><strong>New category for mobile devices</strong></p>
<p>The draft would remove mobile phones from Category IV and establish a new Category VIII, “Mobile Devices”.</p>
<p>Assets classified under the new category would have a maximum annual tax depreciation rate of 50%, meaning mobile phones would not qualify for the proposed 100% accelerated depreciation rate applicable to computers and software.</p>
<p>Automobiles and passenger cars would also remain outside the scope of the accelerated depreciation mechanism.</p>
<p><strong>Gradual implementation</strong></p>
<p>The proposed amendments would introduce a transitional phase between 2027 and 2029 before the full regime took effect.</p>
<p>For Category II assets, the maximum annual depreciation rates would rise to 40% in 2027, 60% in 2028 and 80% in 2029.</p>
<p>For Category IV assets, the corresponding rates would be 60% in 2027, 70% in 2028 and 80% in 2029.</p>
<p>The full 100% maximum depreciation rate would apply from 1 January 2030.</p>
<p>The proposal would distinguish between tax and financial accounting treatment. Accelerated depreciation would apply for tax purposes, while the assets would continue to be depreciated under normal financial accounting rules, including IFRS or national accounting standards.</p>
<p><strong>Proposal modelled on Estonia</strong></p>
<p>The explanatory materials had referred to the Estonian corporate tax model, including Estonia’s 2000 tax reform. Under that approach, profits retained and reinvested in a business are exempt from corporate tax, with taxation arising when profits are distributed, including as dividends.</p>
<p>The Bulgarian proposal sought to provide a similar investment incentive by allowing companies to reduce their taxable profit through accelerated tax depreciation when profits were reinvested in qualifying machinery and production equipment.</p>
<p>The bill’s policy rationale had also cited the need to address declines in Bulgarian industrial production and support the country’s convergence towards average EU income levels.</p>
<p><strong>Fiscal and economic effects</strong></p>
<p>The regulatory impact assessment had identified Bulgarian businesses and private investors undertaking expansion or greenfield projects as the principal affected stakeholders.</p>
<p>The proposal was expected to reduce corporate tax revenues temporarily during the first year as companies made greater use of accelerated depreciation. The assessment indicated that part of this effect could be offset by higher VAT revenues resulting from increased purchases of machinery and other capital equipment.</p>
<p>From the third year onwards, the assessment projected a net-positive effect on total state tax revenues, based on expected economic growth and expansion of the tax base.</p>
<p>The proposed measures would not require administrative reorganisation or the creation of new state agencies.</p>
<p>The assessment also projected that stronger economic growth could contribute to real wage growth, which it linked to improved conditions for domestic demographic stability.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina&#8217;s Tax and Customs Collection and Control Agency (ARCA) has adjusted the collection mechanism for high-value instalments under payment plans, with the aim of streamlining procedures and reducing taxpayers&#8217; administrative burden.</p>
<p>The measure was formalised through <a href="https://servicioscf.afip.gob.ar/publico/sitio/contenido/novedad/ver.aspx?id=5897" target="_blank" rel="noopener">General Resolution 5896/2026</a>, which repeals and amends previous regulations, namely General Resolutions Nos. 5,279, 5,321, 5,525, 5,828 and 5,873.</p>
<p>In light of recent technological and operational updates to the banking network, direct-debit processing has been enabled for transactions that previously required individual electronic fund transfers.</p>
<p><strong>Main changes</strong></p>
<p>Instalments under payment plans for amounts equal to or exceeding ARS 100,000,000 (one hundred million pesos) will be processed directly from the taxpayer&#8217;s bank account through automatic debit collection.</p>
<p>Requests for full early repayment of payment plans will also be processed through the direct-debit system from the bank account.</p>
<p>The requirement to use manual electronic transfers for these instalments — or in exceptional cases where automatic collection fails — has been eliminated.</p>
<p><strong>Requirements for taxpayers</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers with active payment plans managed through the &#8220;Mis Facilidades&#8221; web service must carry out the following checks before the new system takes effect:</p>
<ol>
<li>Check the uniform bank code (CBU): Access the system and verify that the CBU has been correctly declared and registered.</li>
<li>Confirm plan selection: Ensure that the relevant CBU is associated with and selected in the tab for the payment plan currently in progress.</li>
<li>Ensure available funds: Sufficient liquidity must be available in the bank account on the date scheduled for the automatic debit.</li>
</ol>
<p>The new direct-debit collection procedure will become mandatory from 1 October 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Ukraine has joined the Addendum to the Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement on Automatic Exchange of Financial Account Information (Addendum to the CRS MCAA), establishing the international legal basis for exchanging additional information under the updated Common Reporting Standard (CRS).</p>
<p>The Addendum forms an integral part of the Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement and supports the exchange of a broader range of Financial Account Information under the updated CRS and related due diligence procedures.</p>
<p><strong>Expanded tax information</strong></p>
<p>The updated framework will allow Ukraine to receive more complete and structured information from foreign tax authorities concerning financial accounts held abroad by Ukrainian tax residents.</p>
<p>The State Tax Service authorities will be able to use the information to identify undeclared foreign income, establish account holders and controlling persons more accurately, strengthen tax risk analysis and address tax evasion and the transfer of income abroad.</p>
<p>Ukraine&#8217;s accession also supports the alignment of its legislation with international and European standards on tax transparency and administrative cooperation.</p>
<p><strong>Updated CRS framework</strong></p>
<p>The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development approved the updated CRS in 2023 following a review that considered developments in the financial sector, new financial products and practical experience with the standard.</p>
<p>The revisions broadened the CRS scope, clarified reporting requirements and enhanced due diligence procedures, including provisions covering new financial products and instruments that could serve as alternatives to traditional financial products.</p>
<p>The Addendum enables competent authorities that have signed it to exchange the additional information elements required under the updated CRS, subject to the specified conditions and application dates.</p>
<p><strong>Ukraine&#8217;s CRS implementation</strong></p>
<p>Ukraine joined the Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement on Automatic Exchange of Financial Account Information in August 2022 and began participating in international automatic exchange of information under the CRS in 2024.</p>
<p>In 2026, the Ministry of Finance updated Ukraine&#8217;s national CRS rules to reflect the amended international standard. Accession to the Addendum to the CRS MCAA represents a further step in implementing the updated CRS in Ukraine.</p>
<p>The updated rules also support alignment with European Union legislation on administrative cooperation and tax transparency, including changes introduced by Directive DAC8 concerning the CRS.</p>
<p>The implementation of the updated CRS standard in Ukraine is being supported by the European Union Public Finance Management Support Programme for Ukraine (EU4PFM).</p>
<p>Accession to the Addendum does not introduce a new tax or require public disclosure of financial account information. Information received under the framework is to be used for tax purposes covered by international treaties, subject to confidentiality and information protection requirements.</p>

		<title>EU: Parliament approves customs reform targeting e-commerce imports</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/eu-parliament-approves-customs-reform-targeting-e-commerce-imports/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=eu-parliament-approves-customs-reform-targeting-e-commerce-imports</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Abdur Rouf]]></dc:creator>

					<description><![CDATA[The European Parliament approved on 16 September 2026 a major reform of the EU Customs Code that introduced stricter rules for e-commerce imports and established the new EU customs authority (EUCA). The reform will introduce a handling fee for each item bought from non-EU web shops and sent directly to EU consumers. The fee will...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The European Parliament <a href="https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20260911IPR47456/the-european-parliament-adopts-new-e-commerce-and-customs-rules" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved</a> on 16 September 2026 a major reform of the EU Customs Code that introduced stricter rules for e-commerce imports and established the new EU customs authority (EUCA).</p>
<p>The reform will introduce a handling fee for each item bought from non-EU web shops and sent directly to EU consumers. The fee will help cover the costs of managing the growing volume of individual parcels.</p>
<p>The entity responsible for paying other customs charges for the same parcel will also pay the handling fee, avoiding a shift of the cost to consumers. The European Commission will determine the exact amount and revise it every two years to keep it proportional to actual costs. Member states will begin collecting the fee no later than 1 November 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Sellers and platforms to assume importer responsibilities</strong></p>
<p>Sellers and platforms facilitating distance sales of goods from non-EU countries directly to EU customers will be treated as importers under the new rules.</p>
<p>They will be required to provide customs authorities with all required data, pay or guarantee any charges, and ensure that goods shipped to Europe comply with EU laws.</p>
<p>The companies must be established in the EU or represented by an EU-based entity with either authorised economic operator (AEO) or trusted trader status. The requirement is intended to prevent the use of shell companies to circumvent the new rules.</p>
<p>Non-EU country sellers and platforms will also be encouraged to operate warehouses in the EU to facilitate bulk shipments that are easier for customs authorities to check.</p>
<p>Intra-EU client shipments from such warehouses will benefit from a lower handling fee where goods are imported in collective packaging and in quantities large enough to make customs checks more efficient.</p>
<p>Companies that repeatedly fail to comply with EU rules may face fines ranging from 1% to 6% of the total value of goods imported into the EU during the previous 12 months.</p>
<p>Customs authorities may also suspend, revoke, or annul their trusted trader or AEO status and flag them as high-risk operators.</p>
<p><strong>Simplified customs procedures</strong></p>
<p>Import-export companies that comply with the rules and agree to cooperate transparently with customs authorities may qualify for a simplified “trust and check” regime.</p>
<p>Initially, companies will have to undergo vetting and provide customs authorities with access to their electronic systems. In return, their shipments will be subject to fewer checks and they will have greater flexibility over the payment of duties and fees.</p>
<p>The existing AEO qualification will remain available to ensure that customs status remains accessible to smaller economic operators.</p>
<p><strong>EU Data Hub to replace existing systems</strong></p>
<p>The reform will establish a pan-European customs IT system, the EU Data Hub, which will be managed by EUCA.</p>
<p>The system will be available for optional use by 2031 and become mandatory by 2034. It will replace at least 111 software systems currently used by customs authorities across Europe.</p>
<p>For companies, the EU Data Hub is intended to make the declaration of goods and communication with customs authorities easier and faster. For customs authorities, it will support risk analysis through access to comprehensive data and facilitate cross-border cooperation.</p>
<p><strong>New EU customs authority</strong></p>
<p>The reform will also establish EUCA in Lille, France. The authority is expected to become fully operational immediately.</p>
<p>Its main responsibilities will include coordinating future customs cooperation, ensuring risk management and managing the EU Data Hub.</p>
<p><strong>Final approval and implementation</strong></p>
<p>The Council had already given the reform its final formal agreement on 3 September 2026, meaning the European Parliament’s approval represented the final step in the procedure.</p>
<p>The reform will be officially signed into law on Wednesday at 16.00 CEST and published in the EU’s Official Journal as soon as possible. It will enter into force one day later, while member states will have 12 months to begin applying the new rules in full.</p>
<p>Rapporteur Dirk Gotink (EPP, NL) said: “This is the biggest reform of European customs since 1968, supporting trade and the enforcement of EU rules. As rapporteur, I have seen firsthand the tsunami of Chinese parcels violating EU rules, not paying taxes, and overwhelming our customs. We are ending the highly toxic business model of cheap, non-compliant and dangerous imports from China in favour of trade based on our standards and on fairer competition. We are finally giving Europe’s 80,000 customs officers the instruments they need to protect consumers and businesses for the decades to come.”</p>
<p>The European Commission initiated the Customs Code reform in May 2023 in response to the continued growth in individual parcels arriving from non-EU web shops. The Commission said the increasing influx had placed pressure on EU customs authorities and created a route into the EU for unsafe products.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Russian Federal Tax Service has issued clarifications on changes to the rules governing the registration of separate subdivisions and foreign organisations.</p>
<p>Organisations operating through separate subdivisions may now not only select a tax authority for registration at the location of one of them, but also withdraw from the previously chosen authority. The measure applies to subdivisions located within the same municipality, in the federal cities of Moscow, St. Petersburg and Sevastopol, as well as in territories under the jurisdiction of different tax authorities.</p>
<p>Upon receipt of a notification of withdrawal from the chosen tax authority, the subdivision will be registered with the inspection office at the address of its actual location.</p>
<p>Notifications are submitted in the same manner as notifications of choice: in person or through a representative, by registered mail, electronically via telecommunication channels, or through the taxpayer’s personal account. Russian organisations submit such notifications to the tax authority at their place of location, while foreign organisations submit them to the chosen tax authority.</p>
<p>The Federal Tax Service stated that the measure is intended to streamline the registration of organisations with a significant number of subdivisions and to simplify their interaction with tax authorities.</p>
<p>Further changes affect foreign organisations. They are no longer required to submit applications and other documents to the tax authority for registration when opening a bank account. Instead, the application will be submitted directly by the bank where the account is opened, based on the necessary documents.</p>
<p>Information on the registration of the organisation with the tax authority will be sent to the bank that submitted the application, for onward transmission to the foreign organisation. Where required, an extract from the Unified State Register of Taxpayers containing registration data may be issued by the authority directly to the foreign organisation upon request.</p>
<p>According to the Federal Tax Service, the innovation reduces bureaucratic procedures, lowers the administrative burden on foreign organisations, ensures registration on the basis of verified data and increases the efficiency of tax administration.</p>
<p>This <a href="https://www.nalog.gov.ru/rn77/news/activities_fts/16648815/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announcement</a> was made on 11 September 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Uzbekistan published <a href="https://lex.uz/ru/docs/8468724" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Law No. ZRU-1173</a> on 10 September 2026, introducing measures to strengthen regulation of the e-commerce sector.</p>
<p>The new legislation establishes a unified regulatory and taxation framework governing cross-border digital transactions, foreign service providers, online trading platforms, and digital streaming operators. The act also addresses cross-border trade, cybersecurity requirements, and consumer protection by defining subsidiary liability for operators in the event of seller disputes.</p>
<p><strong>VAT and taxation of foreign entities</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Foreign companies providing electronic services or selling goods to individuals in Uzbekistan are subject to VAT where Uzbekistan is the place of sale.</li>
<li>Intermediaries handling payments for foreign sellers generally act as VAT tax agents and must calculate and remit the tax.</li>
<li>Uzbek e-commerce platforms settling payments for foreign sellers are specifically treated as tax agents.</li>
<li>Uzbek legal entities purchasing electronic services from foreign companies generally act as tax agents.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Registration and compliance</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Foreign companies selling directly to individuals must register for VAT, as must intermediaries acting as tax agents.</li>
<li>Registration or deregistration applications must be submitted electronically within 30 calendar days of starting or ending the relevant activities.</li>
<li>Online-platform goods are taxed based on the actual sales price, including VAT.</li>
<li>Tax returns and official filings must be submitted electronically.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Digital operator requirements</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>The law formally recognises e-commerce platform operators, order aggregators, and digital streaming service operators.</li>
<li>Operators must protect personal data and maintain payment and cybersecurity safeguards.</li>
<li>E-commerce platforms and aggregators must verify sellers’ licences and prevent prohibited goods or services from being offered.</li>
<li>Streaming services must protect copyright and prevent unauthorised content distribution.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Consumer protection and liability</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Operators must provide transparency for recommendation and ranking algorithms and allow customers to publish unedited reviews.</li>
<li>Platforms must publish their terms, handle complaints properly, and give at least 30 days’ notice before changing service rules or suspending operations.</li>
<li>Sellers remain primarily responsible for contracts and defective goods, while platforms may have subsidiary liability where sellers fail to meet legitimate customer claims.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Cross-border e-commerce and digital products</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Cross-border e-commerce transactions involving participants or operators in different jurisdictions will follow procedures set by the Cabinet of Ministers.</li>
<li>Digital products imported or exported through digital distribution methods are exempt from customs declaration, with export proceeds credited to the exporter’s account after deducting platform commission fees.</li>
</ul>
<p>The law enters into force three months after its official publication (aligning with 12 December 2026 following publication on 10 September 2026).</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Ukrainian Parliament is reviewing the draft Law on amendments to the tax code of Ukraine regarding further improvement of Transfer Pricing (TP) rules, which was submitted on 4 September 2026. If adopted, the lew would enter into force on 1 January 2028. The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine would have six months from that...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Ukrainian Parliament is reviewing the <a href="https://itd.rada.gov.ua/billinfo/Bills/Card/70692" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft Law</a> on amendments to the tax code of Ukraine regarding further improvement of Transfer Pricing (TP) rules, which was submitted on 4 September 2026.</p>
<p>If adopted, the lew would enter into force on 1 January 2028. The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine would have six months from that date to update related normative and legal acts. The draft would be exempt from the standard regulatory policy procedure under Ukraine&#8217;s obligations under the EU Association Agreement.</p>
<p><strong>Controlled transactions</strong></p>
<p>The draft would expand the scope of controlled transactions under Article 39.2.1 to cover more transactions involving non-resident related parties, foreign commissionaires or agents, non-residents in low-tax jurisdictions or certain legal forms, and non-resident Permanent Establishments (PEs).</p>
<p>Transactions between non-residents and their Ukrainian PEs, Ukrainian residents and their foreign PEs, and transactions between non-resident PEs would also be covered.</p>
<p>Resident related-party transactions would become controlled where the counterparty had accumulated tax losses exceeding EUR 3 million from previous years or used preferential tax regimes.</p>
<p>The definition of a transaction would also include internal calculations between PEs and changes in functions, risks, benefits or opportunities, regardless of whether assets were transferred. Series of operations and multi-party complex arrangements would expressly qualify as controlled transactions.</p>
<p><strong>Arm’s length principle</strong></p>
<p>The arm’s length principle would apply when determining taxable profit from controlled transactions and operations of non-resident PEs.</p>
<p>Tax authorities would be able to recharacterise transactions or replace their terms with alternatives that unrelated parties acting commercially rationally could have agreed upon. Transactions lacking economic reality or an equivalent between unrelated parties could also be disregarded.</p>
<p>Comparability analysis would consider functions, assets and risks, contractual terms, economic and market conditions, business strategies, synergy effects and market characteristics. Realistic alternatives available to the parties would also need to be considered.</p>
<p>TP documentation would have to reflect subsequent events, including legislative changes, force majeure, reorganisations and changes in status. Taxpayers would need to demonstrate &#8220;reasonable efforts&#8221; to establish pricing when transactions were agreed and verify actual outcomes.</p>
<p><strong>Intangible assets and DEMPE</strong></p>
<p>A new definition of intangible assets for TP purposes would cover rights, benefits and results of activities that unrelated parties would not ordinarily transfer without compensation. It would include copyrights, software, inventions, trademarks, goodwill/reputation, know-how, certain unique employee competencies, customer lists and usage rights.</p>
<p>Corporate rights, financial instruments, currency and virtual assets would be excluded.</p>
<p>For intangible asset transactions, functional analysis would have to address Development, Enhancement, Maintenance, Protection, and Exploitation (DEMPE) functions. Legal ownership alone would not establish an entitlement to intellectual property profits where the owner did not perform the relevant DEMPE functions.</p>
<p>Entities providing financing without controlling relevant risks would generally be limited to a risk-free rate of return, while entities controlling financing risks could receive a risk-adjusted return. Where DEMPE functions and associated risks were not properly substantiated, they would be presumed to have been performed or borne in Ukraine.</p>
<p><strong>TP methods and documentation</strong></p>
<p>The Comparable Uncontrolled Price (CUP) method would be expressly treated as the primary and most reliable method where comparable transactions were available.</p>
<p>The interquartile range would apply where comparability uncertainty existed, while the full range would apply where equivalent comparability existed. Adjustments outside the applicable range would generally be made to the median.</p>
<p>For certain transactions involving intangibles, corporate rights, shares, real estate or business transfers where direct comparables were unavailable, the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) Method could be used.</p>
<p>Taxpayers would have 60 calendar days to submit TP documentation following a request from tax authorities. Documentation would need to provide economic justification showing that the parties had acted commercially rationally and considered realistically available alternatives.</p>
<p><strong>Penalties and tax adjustments</strong></p>
<p>A new Article 123² would establish penalties for tax underpayments or reductions in tax losses resulting from TP financial result adjustments under subpoints 140.5.2 and 140.5.21.</p>
<p>The standard penalty would be 7% of the adjustment amount, increasing to 10% where taxpayers also failed to submit TP reports, the Master File, CbC reports or TP documentation.</p>
<p>A 15% penalty would apply in specified aggravating circumstances, including misrepresentation or non-disclosure of facts, improper selection of the TP method, analysed party or comparables, failure to account for a series of transactions, or insufficient DEMPE justification.</p>
<p>Article 120 would also introduce penalties for inaccurate information in CbC reports, the Master File, TP documentation and CbC notifications. Daily penalties would apply for failure to submit CbC reports or notifications after 30 days.</p>
<p>Under proposed Article 140 amendments, subpoint 140.5.2 would cover taxable profit not received because of non-arm&#8217;s length conditions, while subpoint 140.5.21 would cover transactions disregarded or recharacterised under subpoint 39.2.2.12.</p>
<p>Article 141.4.2 would impose 18% non-resident income tax on relevant TP adjustment amounts where tax had not been withheld at payment, unless an international treaty provided another rate. The tax would be payable by 1 October following the reporting year.</p>
<p>Separate rules would also apply to controlled transactions conducted by JIIs or non-state pension funds, with the TP adjustment spread subject to the standard CIT rate.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Inland Revenue Board of Malaysia (IRBM) released <a href="https://www.hasil.gov.my/wp-content/uploads/IRBM-e-Invoice-Specific-Guideline.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">version 4.9 of its e-Invoice Specific Guideline</a> on 7 September 2026.</p>
<p>The update introduces simpler identification rules for businesses issuing invoices to individual buyers, addressing the practical difficulties of collecting Tax Identification Numbers during transactions.</p>
<p><strong>Flexible options for individual buyers</strong></p>
<p>Under Section 3.5.4 of the guideline, businesses can now accept one of three identification formats from individual buyers. Malaysian citizens holding MyKad or MyTentera cards can provide their Tax Identification Number alone, their identification number alone, or both. Foreign residents with MyPR or MyKAS documents follow the same three options.</p>
<p>Non-Malaysian individuals without residency documents have two pathways. They can supply an IRBM-assigned Tax Identification Number paired with their passport number. If no IRBM number exists, businesses may use the General Foreign Buyer TIN (EI00000000020) listed in Appendix 1 along with the passport number.</p>
<p><strong>System input standards</strong></p>
<p>When businesses receive partial identification data, the IRBM prescribes standard system values. If only a Tax Identification Number arrives, the supplier enters &#8220;000000000000&#8221; into the registration field. When only a MyKad or similar document number is provided, the system receives the General Public TIN (EI00000000010) as the buyer&#8217;s Tax Identification Number. For passport-only submissions from non-Malaysians, the Foreign Buyer TIN (EI00000000020) gets entered into the system.</p>
<p>Regardless of which identification route is used, businesses must still collect the individual buyer&#8217;s full name, residential address, contact telephone number, and SST registration number (or mark it &#8220;NA&#8221; if unregistered). These requirements appear in Table 3.1 of the guideline.</p>
<p><strong>Broader application across transactions</strong></p>
<p>The concession extends beyond simple retail sales. It applies to individual shipping recipients listed in invoice annexures under Table 3.2. High-value transactions exceeding MYR 10,000 (starting January 2026) and restricted industries, including automotive sales and flight tickets, can use these flexible options when issuing individual invoices rather than consolidated monthly statements under Section 3.7.</p>
<p>Self-billed e-invoices under Section 8.7 benefit from the same framework. When businesses pay individual suppliers, agents, dealers, or distributors who lack formal business registration, they apply identical identification options.</p>
<p>The concession also covers periodic billing from utilities, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and telecommunications companies under Section 4.2.7. E-commerce platforms issuing invoices to individual buyers or accepting self-billed invoices from individual merchants use these same rules under Section 14.4.6.</p>
<p>The update aligns with the Income Tax Act 1967 and reduces compliance friction across Malaysia&#8217;s digital invoicing ecosystem.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[New Zealand Inland Revenue updated its guidance on 9 September 2026 on the application of the Pillar Two GloBE Rules to multinational enterprise (MNE) groups with a constituent entity in New Zealand. The GloBE rules apply to MNE groups with global annual revenue exceeding EUR 750 million in at least two of the previous four...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>New Zealand Inland Revenue updated its <a href="https://www.ird.govt.nz/international-tax/business/nz-globe-rules-and-inclusive-framework-2-pillar-solution/the-globe-rules" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance</a> on 9 September 2026 on the application of the Pillar Two GloBE Rules to multinational enterprise (MNE) groups with a constituent entity in New Zealand.</p>
<p>The GloBE rules apply to MNE groups with global annual revenue exceeding EUR 750 million in at least two of the previous four years where the group has a constituent entity in New Zealand. The rules apply to fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025.</p>
<p>The ultimate parent entity’s (UPE) fiscal year end determines the deadlines for GloBE registration and other filing requirements.</p>
<p><strong>GloBE registration</strong></p>
<p>A designated New Zealand constituent entity must register a GloBE account for the MNE group within six months of the end of the first fiscal year to which the GloBE rules apply.</p>
<p>Only one registration is required for each MNE group, covering all its constituent entities in New Zealand. The designated New Zealand constituent entity must identify all New Zealand constituent entities as part of the registration.</p>
<p>For example, an MNE group with a fiscal year ending on 31 December 2025 must register by 30 June 2026. For a 31 March 2026 year end, the deadline is 30 September 2026, while an MNE with a 30 June 2026 year end must register by 31 December 2026.</p>
<p>Registration is required even where an MNE group is within the scope of the rules for only part of a fiscal year, including where it is disposing of or dissolving its New Zealand operations.</p>
<p>Joint ventures accounted for under the equity method in an MNE group’s consolidated financial statements should not be included as constituent entities in the registration. Their details will instead be provided in the GloBE information return (GIR).</p>
<p>Joint ventures consolidated on a line-by-line basis should be included in the registration. A New Zealand permanent establishment of an entity included in the MNE group’s consolidated financial statements on a line-by-line basis is also treated as a separate constituent entity for registration purposes.</p>
<p>Failure to register or provide an accurate notification could result in a penalty of up to NZD 100,000.</p>
<p><strong>Side-by-Side Package</strong></p>
<p>New Zealand has adopted changes to the GloBE rules under the Side-by-Side (SbS) Package published by the OECD on 5 January 2026.</p>
<p>The Simplified ETR Safe Harbour and Substance-based Tax Incentive Safe Harbour are available for fiscal years commencing on or after 1 January 2026.</p>
<p>The Transitional CbCR Safe Harbour has been extended for an additional year. It covers fiscal years beginning on or before 31 December 2027, but does not apply to a fiscal year ending after 30 June 2029.</p>
<p>The Side-by-Side Safe Harbour and UPE Safe Harbour are available for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2026 for MNEs with a fixed-date fiscal year end, such as 31 December.</p>
<p>For MNEs using a 52- or 53-week fiscal year ending on the same day of the week each year, the safe harbours are available for fiscal years starting on or after 26 December 2025.</p>
<p><strong>GloBE notifications and information returns</strong></p>
<p>As part of registration, the designated constituent entity provides information covering all New Zealand constituent entities of the MNE group. This information forms part of a standing notification.</p>
<p>Changes to the notification must be made within six months of the end of the fiscal year. These changes can include the fiscal year end, GloBE Information Return (GIR) filing responsibility and GIR filer details.</p>
<p>MNE groups can also update information about the UPE and New Zealand constituent entities, including adding, editing or removing records.</p>
<p>If the designated New Zealand constituent entity changes, the existing entity must de-register and the new designated New Zealand constituent entity must register.</p>
<p>For New Zealand-headquartered MNEs, the GIR will be filed in New Zealand by the designated New Zealand constituent entity. For MNEs headquartered outside New Zealand, the GIR may be filed in New Zealand or overseas by a constituent entity in another implementing jurisdiction that will exchange the return with New Zealand.</p>
<p>The GIR can be filed in New Zealand 18 months after the end of the first fiscal year to which New Zealand’s GloBE rules apply. New Zealand-headquartered MNEs may need to file within 15 months of the first applicable fiscal year where they are already subject to GloBE rules in other jurisdictions.</p>
<p>The GIR must be submitted electronically through myIR in XML format meeting the requirements of the OECD GIR XML Schema. Information exchanged between jurisdictions will depend on the MNE group’s structure and how the GloBE rules apply in each jurisdiction, including the income inclusion rule (IIR), undertaxed payments rule (UTPR) and qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT).</p>
<p><strong>Top-up tax returns</strong></p>
<p>The designated New Zealand constituent entity will be required to file the multinational top-up tax return through myIR. The online return is expected to become available from April 2027.</p>
<p>The return will require the relevant fiscal year end, the conversion rate used between the GIR and top-up tax return, and the amount of top-up tax payable, split between IIR, DIIR and UTPR. All top-up tax amounts must be reported in New Zealand dollars.</p>
<p>IIR and UTPR top-up taxes apply for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025, while DIIR top-up tax applies for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2026.</p>
<p>For the first fiscal year to which the rules apply, the top-up tax return will be due 20 months after the fiscal year end. For subsequent years, the deadline will be 16 months after the fiscal year ends.</p>
<p><strong>Proposed remedial legislation</strong></p>
<p>Inland Revenue also outlined proposed remedial legislation affecting top-up tax return filing.</p>
<p>The proposals would provide for a single top-up tax return by the designated constituent entity covering all New Zealand constituent entities. They would also remove the requirement to file a top-up tax return where there is no top-up tax liability and clarify how the time bar applies.</p>
<p>The updated guidance has therefore set out the current registration, notification and filing framework for MNE groups within the scope of New Zealand’s GloBE rules, together with the applicable deadlines and proposed changes to the top-up tax return process.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Canada: Supreme Court rejects Husky Energy bid to challenge dividend tax ruling</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/canada-supreme-court-rejects-husky-energy-bid-to-challenge-dividend-tax-ruling/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=canada-supreme-court-rejects-husky-energy-bid-to-challenge-dividend-tax-ruling</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 13:26:35 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Non-resident companies]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Withholding tax]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Withholding taxes due]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Americas]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Canada]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=88060</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The Supreme Court of Canada has dismissed Husky Energy Inc.&#8217;s application for leave to appeal on 3 September 2026. The decision upholds a 2025 Federal Court of Appeal ruling that blocked the company from using a tax treaty loophole to reduce withholding taxes on dividend payments. The outcome closes a significant chapter in Canadian tax...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Supreme Court of Canada has <a href="https://www.scc-csc.ca/cases-dossiers/search-recherche/42116/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">dismissed</a> Husky Energy Inc.&#8217;s application for leave to appeal on 3 September 2026. The decision upholds a 2025 Federal Court of Appeal ruling that blocked the company from using a tax treaty loophole to reduce withholding taxes on dividend payments. The outcome closes a significant chapter in Canadian tax litigation over beneficial ownership and treaty shopping.</p>
<p><strong>The Luxembourg conduit structure</strong></p>
<p>In 2003, Husky Energy declared a substantial dividend to its shareholders. Three Barbados-based corporations held more than 70% of the company&#8217;s shares. Each of these Barbados firms temporarily loaned its shares to Luxembourg corporations under standard Securities Lending Agreements. The Luxembourg companies received the gross dividend, then returned the shares to the Barbados firms along with the funds.</p>
<p>The Luxembourg tax authorities issued a ruling stating that the Luxembourg corporations were mere conduits for the dividends and bore no tax liability in Luxembourg. This arrangement appeared designed to exploit the lower withholding tax rate available under the Canada-Luxembourg treaty compared to the Canada-Barbados treaty.</p>
<p><strong>The withholding tax dispute</strong></p>
<p>Husky Energy withheld 5% tax on the dividends, citing the Canada-Luxembourg tax treaty rate applicable to Luxembourg residents. The Canada-Barbados treaty establishes a 15% withholding rate, while corporations without treaty coverage face a standard 25% withholding rate under Canadian law.</p>
<p>The Minister of National Revenue assessed the company for underpaying withholding taxes. The Minister&#8217;s position held that the Barbados corporations remained the beneficial owners and the 15% rate applied, regardless of the temporary share lending arrangement.</p>
<p><strong>Court decisions and legal reasoning</strong></p>
<p>The Tax Court of Canada examined the substance of the transaction rather than its form. The court found that the Luxembourg corporations assumed no financial risk and did not hold the dividends for their own benefit or use. Based on this analysis, the court determined the Luxembourg firms were not the beneficial owners and dismissed Husky Energy&#8217;s appeal.</p>
<p>The Federal Court of Appeal reviewed the Tax Court decision and found no errors in the beneficial ownership analysis. The appellate court confirmed that the Barbados corporations were the actual beneficial owners under tax law, making the 15% withholding rate the correct obligation.</p>
<p><strong>Final outcome</strong></p>
<p>Husky Energy&#8217;s attempt to reach the Supreme Court of Canada failed when the court dismissed the leave to appeal application. The dismissal leaves the lower court decisions final and binding. The ruling affirms that tax treaty benefits cannot be claimed through temporary conduit arrangements that lack genuine economic substance.</p>

<p><strong>Corporate adjustments</strong></p>
<p>From 2027, embedded currency hedging results on participation investments will no longer qualify for the participation exemption.</p>
<p><strong>Tax changes for entrepreneurs and businesses</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Carbon and waste tax timelines pushed back:</strong> The Netherlands has postponed its industrial CO2 levy target from 2030 to 2035 (EUR 304 per ton for waste incineration plants) and cut the waste tax increase to EUR 23.75 per ton in 2028, down from EUR 53.25 per ton.</li>
<li><strong>Forestry exemption abolished:</strong> The forestry profit exemption ends on 1 January 2029, generating EUR 34 million that year and EUR 35 million annually after.</li>
<li><strong>Pillar Two safe harbours introduced:</strong> Pillar 2 safe harbour rules (including Side-by-Side, UPE, and Simplified ETR provisions) take effect retroactively from 2026 under the Wetsvoorstel Wet aanvullende veiligehavenregels Wet minimumbelasting 2024.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Innovation and sustainability measures</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Expansion of innovation Box SME lump-sum cap: </strong>The lump-sum threshold for the SME innovation box increases from EUR 25,000 to EUR 100,000 per year starting 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Real estate transfer tax reduction for investors:</strong> The transfer tax rate for residential properties not used as a primary residence (investors/landlords) is reduced from 8% to 7% from 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Transfer tax exemption for social housing corporations:</strong> A targeted transfer tax exemption is created for social housing (DAEB) property transfers between housing associations effective 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Energy investment allowance:</strong> EIA deduction increases from 40% to 45.5% from 1 January 2027 to encourage business energy efficiency.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Measures for start-up entrepreneurs</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Employee stock options:</strong> Tax rules will be simplified and deferred from 2027 under measures for startups and scale-ups.</li>
<li><strong>Start-up deduction: </strong>The deduction falls to EUR 10 in 2027 and will be abolished from 1 January 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Accelerated depreciation: </strong>The special accelerated depreciation scheme for startups will end on 1 January 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Disability start-up deduction: </strong>The deduction for disabled entrepreneurs will be abolished from 1 January 2029 due to low use and high administrative costs.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Tax changes for products and services </strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Fuel excise duty: </strong>Temporary petrol excise relief is extended to 31 December 2027.</li>
<li>Flight tax: Distance-based rates begin in 2027, with the highest rate reduced to EUR 59.43 per passenger from 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Alcohol excise duty: </strong>Inflation indexation starts from 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Small breweries: </strong>The 7.5% excise duty discount for small independent breweries will end from 1 January 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Tap water tax: </strong>The tax will rise by EUR 0.10 per m³ from 1 January 2027 to EUR 0.537 per m³.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>VAT rate alignments</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Floriculture VAT:</strong> VAT on flowers and plants will increase from 9% to 21% from 1 January 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Hot air ballooning VAT:</strong> Balloon flights will move from 9% to 21% VAT from 1 January 2028.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Motor vehicle &amp; transport taxes</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Youngtimer scheme:</strong> Existing users retain current tax treatment for one additional year in 2027, while the eligibility age threshold will be reduced to 20 years from 2029.</li>
<li><strong>Motor vehicle tax relief: </strong>Entrepreneur delivery vans receive a 50% MRB reduction, while heavy goods vehicles receive a zero rate for the second half of 2026.</li>
<li><strong>Truck charge: </strong>Truck charge rates are reduced by 22.3% from 1 September to 31 December 2026 to offset higher fuel costs.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Individual income tax measures </strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Higher tax-free travel allowance: </strong>The maximum tax-free travel allowance will rise from EUR 0.23 to EUR 0.25 per kilometre, retroactive to 1 January 2026.</li>
<li><strong>Pension accrual cap frozen: </strong>The EUR 137,800 income cap for tax-favoured pension and annuity accrual will remain unchanged from 2027 through 2032.</li>
<li><strong>Staff discount exemption abolished: </strong>The EUR 500 annual tax-free exemption for employee discounts on employer-produced goods will be abolished from 1 January 2027.</li>
<li><strong>Healthcare cost deduction abolished:</strong> The income tax deduction for specific healthcare expenses will be fully abolished from 1 January 2028, reducing compliance burdens and raising additional revenue.</li>
</ul>

<p>Under Law 2569 on Successions and Donations, the taxable base of the inheritance tax (impuesto sobre sucesiones) is the total estate left by the deceased, including movable and immovable property and duly documented rights and obligations. The tax is charged at 3% of the net hereditary mass after permitted deductions under articles 4 and 6.</p>
<p>The DGII confirmed that Law 171-07 benefits apply during the lifetime of the principal pensioner or rentier. These include an exemption from transfer tax on the first property acquired, 50% relief from mortgage tax and real estate property tax (IPI) where applicable, an exemption from tax on dividends and interest of any source, and 50% capital gains relief subject to specified conditions.</p>
<p>The benefits do not exempt the deceased’s estate from inheritance tax. However, certain incentives may continue after the death of the principal beneficiary for the spouse and dependants defined in article 5 of Law 171-07, provided they also meet the qualifying conditions under article 17.</p>
<p>The eligible dependants can include unmarried minor children, disabled adult children, university-enrolled adult children who remain economically dependent on the deceased, and qualifying minors under legal guardianship. The DGII stated that beneficiaries seeking continued incentives must satisfy the documentation and compliance requirements applicable under Law 171-07.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan’s Southern Area National Taxation Bureau had <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/singlehtml/384fb3077bb349ea973e7fc6f13b6974?cntId=708e376e505d4b128a64fa8696070162" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reminded</a> businesses on 16 September 2026, that travel expenses claimed for tax purposes must be supported by evidence showing that the trips were related to business operations.</p>
<p>Under Article 38 of the Income Tax Act and Article 62 of the Guidelines for the Examination of Corporate Income Tax Returns, expenses unrelated to a company’s principal or ancillary business activities cannot be recognised as deductible expenses or losses. Paragraph 1 of Article 74 further requires businesses to provide business trip reports detailing daily destinations, parties contacted and the nature of business activities, along with relevant supporting documents.</p>
<p>The bureau said transportation and accommodation receipts alone may not be sufficient. Businesses should also retain evidence such as invitation letters, email correspondence, meeting notices and exhibition photographs to establish the business purpose of trips.</p>
<p>In a recent examination of a company’s 2023 corporate income tax return, the bureau found that approximately TWD 800,000 in travel expenses had been claimed for a Europe trip by the company’s responsible person and shareholders. Although air ticket stubs and hotel receipts had been provided, the business trip report only stated “market research”.</p>
<p>The company was unable to provide details of the parties visited, business negotiation records, correspondence with potential local customers or relevant contracts. As it could not demonstrate that the trip was connected to its business operations, the bureau disallowed the claimed travel expenses and assessed additional tax.</p>
<p>The bureau advised businesses to strengthen internal controls by requiring employees to record their daily business activities during trips and retain business discussion records, emails and other supporting documents together with accounting vouchers.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic’s Executive Power had submitted the draft Application Regulation for Law No. 30-26 for <a href="https://www.consultoria.gov.do/consultas/publicas/consulta-publica-borrador-reglamento-de-aplicacion-de-la-ley-num-30-26-sobre-medidas-pro-crecimiento-economico-simplificacion-fiscal-y-mitigacion-de-la-crisis-internacional-3068" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a>, setting out rules on tax procedures, incentive regimes, withholding taxes and other administrative measures.</p>
<p>The consultation was open from 7 September to 8 October 2026. Questions and comments could be submitted through the “submit comments” form accompanying the publication.</p>
<p><strong>Tax incentives</strong></p>
<p>The draft regulation provided that a single tax-generating event, economic activity, investment or operation could not benefit from more than one special tax incentive regime.</p>
<p>Taxpayers conducting separate economic activities or investments could access different incentive regimes if they maintained separate accounting identifying the revenues, costs, expenses, assets and liabilities of each activity.</p>
<p>The Ministry of Finance and Economy could request the Executive Power to object to a taxpayer’s incentive classification where a technical report showed that the investment:</p>
<ul>
<li>Failed to meet the objectives of the law;</li>
<li>Generated tax expenditure exceeding its social benefit;</li>
<li>Created unfair competition or market distortions;</li>
<li>Was profitable without the incentive; or</li>
<li>Failed to generate wider economic effects.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Tax appeals and debt consignment</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers challenging a tax debt administratively or judicially could consign the disputed amount with the tax administration, DGII.</p>
<p>DGII would be required to accept the consignment and could not apply precautionary collection measures. Consignment would immediately suspend late-payment surcharges and indemnity interest.</p>
<p>If the debt became res judicata, the consigned amount would extinguish the tax obligation. If the debt were annulled or reduced, the taxpayer could initiate a refund procedure for an undue or excess payment.</p>
<p><strong>Payment agreements and audit discounts</strong></p>
<p>DGII would assess payment agreement requests based on the taxpayer’s payment capacity, the amount of debt, tax compliance history and the sufficiency of guarantees offered.</p>
<p>The draft also proposed:</p>
<ul>
<li>90% reduction: For voluntary tax return rectifications made without a prior tax authority determination or requirement.</li>
<li>70% discount: Where the taxpayer requested the discount within 20 business days of receiving a potential debt notice and accepted the identified tax determinations.</li>
</ul>
<p>Payment under the latter procedure would complete the audit and result in a “no fiscal interest” certificate.</p>
<p>The statute of limitations would also be suspended for delinquent debt where a return was filed without timely payment, or where an audit debt became res judicata and remained unpaid.</p>
<p><strong>Income tax rules</strong></p>
<p>Residents would remain subject to tax on Dominican-source income and foreign-source income derived from investments, financial gains and technical assistance.</p>
<p>The draft regulation defined technical assistance as independent services provided locally or from abroad that supplied specialised knowledge, experience or skills through non-patentable procedures or techniques, including associated training.</p>
<p>Excluded services would include teaching, employee services, foreign trade or customs-transparent costs, travel reimbursements, intellectual property or equipment transfers, administrative execution without knowledge transfer, technical opinions without ongoing training and standardised mass digital services such as streaming, digital advertising and marketplaces.</p>
<p><strong>Digital assets and software</strong></p>
<p>Digital assets and cryptoassets would be defined as digital representations of value or rights based on Distributed Ledger Technology or similar cryptographic mechanisms. The definition would include stablecoins, non-fungible tokens (NFTs) and crypto derivatives.</p>
<p>The draft distinguished royalties from software transactions. Payments for the use of patentable intangible assets or industrial or scientific equipment would constitute royalties, while software licences would be excluded.</p>
<p>Software licences would cover rights to use or exploit software where the licensor retained copyright. Periodic fees, subscriptions and usage-based payments would be presumed to constitute licences.</p>
<p>A software acquisition would instead involve a full, permanent and irrevocable transfer of the economic rights to the copyright.</p>
<p><strong>Foreign tax credits</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers claiming credits for foreign tax withholdings would need to substantiate the claim by providing evidence of actual tax payment abroad, contracts or DGII-compliant invoices and proof of payment through reliable financial channels.</p>
<p>Withholding tax measures</p>
<p>The draft established several withholding rules, including a 15% withholding on a presumed net income equal to 20% of gross value, resulting in an effective 3% withholding, for:</p>
<ul>
<li>Cargo and passenger transportation services;</li>
<li>Certain non-personal services, including cleaning, fumigation, electrical and mechanical repairs, masonry, carpentry, painting and plumbing;</li>
<li>Civil construction contractors covering roads, aqueducts and buildings; and</li>
<li>Transfers of registrable movable property.</li>
</ul>
<p>A 15% ISR withholding on rental income would apply only where the tenant was a legal entity or organisation and the landlord was an individual receiving rent directly.</p>
<p>State suppliers authorised as electronic issuers and invoicing through E-CF would be exempt from the standard 5% ISR withholding.</p>
<p>A temporary 30% withholding rate would apply during fiscal years 2026, 2027 and 2028 to Dominican-source income payments of at least DOP 1,000,000,000.00 made to non-residents.</p>
<p><strong>Primary residence and capital gains</strong></p>
<p>The draft defined a primary residence as an individual’s physical, continuous main home.</p>
<p>The property would generally need to correspond to the seller’s RNC address, have a Title Certificate and active basic utility contracts, and have been continuously occupied for at least three years before the transfer.</p>
<p>Commercial, rental and vacation properties would be excluded.</p>
<p>For capital gains reinvestment into a new primary residence to qualify for exemption, the transaction would need to satisfy three conditions:</p>
<ol>
<li>Full or partial payment in accordance with the contract, supported by evidence;</li>
<li>Payment of the 3% Real Estate Transfer Tax to DGII; and</li>
<li>Formal deposit and registration of the title transfer with the Title Registry.</li>
</ol>
<p>Pre-sale contracts, purchase options and unregistered private acts would not qualify.</p>
<p><strong>Advance tax payments</strong></p>
<p>Companies exceeding MSME revenue limits during a fiscal year would retain their existing advance payment schedule until the end of that year. The new classification would apply from the following fiscal year.</p>
<p>DGII could authorise full or partial reductions in advance payments where taxpayers demonstrated force majeure or exceptional circumstances.</p>
<p><strong>ITBIS and other tax measures</strong></p>
<p>Manufacturers of ITBIS-exempt goods could choose, for each purchase, either exemption through approval of a proforma invoice or payment of ITBIS followed by a tax credit. Both mechanisms could not be used for the same purchase.</p>
<p>Tax benefits and exemptions for life insurance would apply only to the life portion of premiums. Combined policies would therefore need to separately identify premiums attributable to life coverage.</p>
<p>The LPG contribution rate would be fixed at USD 174.50 per metric ton based on import parity pricing formulas.</p>
<p><strong>Accelerated depreciation</strong></p>
<p>The proposed regulation would expand the definition of “industrial use” for accelerated depreciation.</p>
<p>The definition would cover assets directly, habitually and necessarily used in production, transformation or technical service activities in sectors including commercial, healthcare, agro-industrial, shopping centre and power generation operations.</p>
<p>Medical, surgical, optical, measuring and precision instruments under Customs Tariff Chapter 90 could qualify where they complemented machinery under Chapters 84 or 85 or served as primary operational equipment.</p>
<p>Taxpayers would need to provide technical descriptions, customs tariff classifications, purchase invoices, payment evidence and written justification of industrial use.</p>
<p><strong>Inheritance and asset valuation</strong></p>
<p>The proposed rules would establish specific valuation methods for inherited assets.</p>
<p>Real estate would be valued at the higher of the cadastral value or DGII reference value. Vehicles and movable goods would use the DGII reference price or an official expert appraisal.</p>
<p>Bank accounts and publicly traded securities would be valued using certified balances or the stock exchange closing price on the date of death.</p>
<p>Private shares would be valued using the net book value or equity balance from the last closed fiscal year.</p>
<p><strong>Donations and property transfers</strong></p>
<p>Transfers of property between relatives would be assessed based on evidence including payment, third-party financing and market price references.</p>
<p>Where such indicators existed, the transaction could be treated as a taxable sale rather than a tax-exempt donation. Transfers between spouses would generally receive neutral tax treatment unless they arose from divorce.</p>
<p><strong>Transit passengers</strong></p>
<p>Passengers in transit who remained in the Dominican Republic for less than 24 hours without formally entering through immigration would be exempt from airport departure contributions.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

<p><strong>How the mechanism works</strong></p>
<p>Law no. 162/2026 created a dynamic system that reviews fuel market indicators every two weeks. The Ministry adjusts the excise duty reduction based on international quotations and domestic pump prices. This approach aims to shield transport and logistics sectors from sudden cost spikes and prevent fuel costs from pushing consumer prices higher across the broader economy.</p>
<p>The Ministry of Finance will continue tracking international prices and domestic market conditions.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Angola’s taxation authority, the General Tax Administration (AGT) has <a href="https://portaldocontribuinte.minfin.gov.ao/noticia?id=985597" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced </a>on 27 August 2026 that taxpayers under the general regime must settle their provisional industrial tax for the 2026 fiscal year by 31 August 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Calculation method and rate</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers apply a rate of 2% to the total volume of sales of goods and services not subject to withholding tax during the first six months of 2026. This calculation follows Article 66 of the Industrial Tax Code, established under Law No. 19/14 (22 October 2014) and amended by Law No. 26/20 (20 July 2020).</p>
<p>Sales already subject to withholding obligations are excluded from this calculation, as withholding payments already contribute to the taxpayer&#8217;s annual tax obligation. The taxable amount must be reported in the &#8220;Taxable Value&#8221; field when filing the settlement.</p>
<p><strong>Special cases and exemptions</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers who reported losses in the previous tax year remain exempt from the provisional settlement requirement. However, the AGT requires them to submit a declaration through the Taxpayer Portal to formally report this status and maintain compliance records.</p>
<p><strong>Supervised financial and insurance entities</strong></p>
<p>Entities regulated by the BNA (banking sector), ARSEG (insurance sector), ISJ (financial services), or CMC (gaming sector) follow a different calculation method. These organisations apply the same 2% rate to the total result from financial intermediation operations, insurance and reinsurance premiums, or gaming activities generated during the first six months of the prior financial year. Capital gains income is excluded from this calculation to prevent double taxation.</p>
<p><strong>Filing requirements</strong></p>
<p>The AGT directs all submissions through the Taxpayer Portal at<a href="https://portaldocontribuinte.minfin.gov.ao" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> https://portaldocontribuinte.minfin.gov.ao</a>.  Filers log in with their credentials and navigate to Declarations, then Industrial Tax, then Provisional Settlement.</p>
<p>Once the voluntary deadline passes, the AGT will identify taxpayers in default or those with inconsistencies in their submitted information and issue notifications accordingly.</p>

BIR Commissioner Charlito Martin R. Mendoza issued the circular to provide guidance on how qualified Export-Oriented Enterprises (EOEs) handle Value-Added Tax refund claims during a defined transition period.</p>
<p>The circular addresses a specific gap in Section III(1)(a) of RMC No. 37-2025. It clarifies which input taxes EOEs may recover as the government shifted EOE certification authority to the Department of Trade and Industry-Export Marketing Bureau.</p>
<p><strong>New refund window for transitional period</strong></p>
<p>The transitory period runs from 28 November 2024 through 31 December 2025. This window aligns with the effective date of Republic Act No. 12066, commonly known as the CREATE MORE Act.</p>
<p>EOEs that obtained their DTI-EMB zero-rating certificates during this timeframe may claim VAT refunds for passed-on taxes. The refund period extends from 28 November 2024 until the specific date each enterprise received its certification certificate.</p>
<p>The DTI-EMB issued these certificates on varying dates. Records show certificates were issued from as early as 14 May 2025 to as late as 26 December 2025. This variance prompted the need for clearer refund parameters.</p>
<p><strong>Documentary requirements separate by filing date</strong></p>
<p>The BIR revised its supporting document checklist requirements to account for different filing periods. The revision splits compliance obligations based on when claims are submitted.</p>
<p>Enterprises that filed refund claims before 1 April 2025 must submit documentation under Annex A.1.1 of the amended circular. Those filing from 1 April 2025 onwards follow Annex A.1.2. This separation reflects regulatory changes that took effect on 10 April 2025, when the BIR originally issued RMC No. 37-2025.</p>
<p>The DTI published its own Department Administrative Order No. 25-03 on 28 March 2025 to establish the certification framework for these enterprises.</p>
<p><strong>Consequences of missing the certification deadline</strong></p>
<p>Enterprises that reached the 70% export sales threshold but failed to secure DTI-EMB certification by 31 December 2025 face restrictions. These entities cannot claim a cash VAT refund in the immediately following taxable year.</p>
<p>However, the regulation does not eliminate their input tax entitlement. Unused input VAT balances may carry forward to subsequent quarters. Enterprises may apply these carried-forward amounts against future VAT liabilities under standard tax provisions.</p>
<p>The circular reinforces that all refund claims must meet Section 112 requirements of the Philippine Tax Code. Only input taxes directly attributable to zero-rated export sales qualify for recovery. The BIR will not process refunds where the input tax has already been reimbursed, credited, or used elsewhere.</p>
<p>The circular took effect immediately upon publication on 7 September 2026.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued new guidance on tax relief for farmers and ranchers across the country who sold or exchanged livestock due to severe drought on 15 September 2026. The extension allows affected producers to defer taxes on gains from forced livestock sales and take additional time to replace their animals. Who...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) <a href="https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-announces-extension-of-tax-relief-for-farmers-and-ranchers-affected-by-drought-in-49-states-other-regions" target="_blank" rel="noopener">issued</a> new guidance on tax relief for farmers and ranchers across the country who sold or exchanged livestock due to severe drought on 15 September 2026. The extension allows affected producers to defer taxes on gains from forced livestock sales and take additional time to replace their animals.</p>
<p><strong>Who qualifies for the relief </strong></p>
<p>Eligible farmers and ranchers must meet two conditions: the livestock must have been held for draft, dairy, or breeding purposes, and the sale or exchange must have occurred in an area with a federal drought designation. Livestock raised for slaughter or held for sporting purposes do not qualify for this relief. Sales of poultry also fall outside the program&#8217;s scope.</p>
<p><strong>Timeline for livestock replacement</strong></p>
<p>The standard tax rule requires farmers to replace sold livestock within two years. Notice 2026-54 extends this replacement period to four years for eligible producers in drought-affected areas. If drought conditions continue, the IRS can extend the deadline further.</p>
<p>The extended deadline also includes a provision that gives farmers until the end of their first tax year after the first drought-free year to complete the replacement. For producers whose original four-year window was set to close at the end of 2026, this means they now have until the end of their next tax year to replace the livestock.</p>
<p><strong>Geographic scope and determination</strong></p>
<p>The relief covers 49 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and other designated areas. Qualification depends on whether the region received a federal drought designation during the 12 months ending 31 August 2026. The National Drought Mitigation Centre identifies regions experiencing exceptional, extreme, or severe drought between 1 September 2025 and 31 August 2026.</p>
<p>IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano stated that the extension provides support to farmers and ranchers facing ongoing drought hardship. Full details and examples appear in <a href="https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-06-82.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Notice 2006-82</a>, available on IRS.gov.</p>
